Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space ([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]), let $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an inertial frame with inertial chart $x:A\to\mathbb R^4$ ([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]), let $c>0$ be the framework's conversion constant, and let $\delta$ be the Euclidean spatial form of that frame on $n^\perp$, $n:=e_0$, with norm $|\cdot|$ and positive spatial orientation ([[def-spatial-euclidean-structure-of-an-inertial-frame]])

Adopt the SI system of units for this framework, with the following quantity table and conventions; every symbol is a quantity of this framework and the laboratory structure is that of [[def-em-lab-geometry]]. (a) [Coordinates and constants] $x^0=ct$ and each spatial coordinate $x^i$ carries the metre (m); the time coordinate $t$ carries the second (s); the conversion constant $c>0$ carries m s$^{-1}$ and has the exact SI defining value $c=299\,792\,458\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; the elementary charge $e$ has the exact SI defining value $e=1.602\,176\,634\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$, and this item does not assert that physical charge is quantised; the magnetic constant $\mu_0>0$ carries N A$^{-2}$ and is measured, so no exact numerical value of $\mu_0$ is asserted. The pre-2019 SI fixed the historical nominal $\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}:=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{H\,m^{-1}} =4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-2}}$ exactly; since the revised SI took effect on 20 May 2019, $\mu_0$ is experimentally determined. The SI brochure quotes the nominal $\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}$ as the estimate at the 2019 adoption with relative standard uncertainty $2.3\times10^{-10}$; this is historical estimate and uncertainty context, not an exact equality for the actual $\mu_0$ or a current measured value. The electric constant is defined within the framework by $$\varepsilon_0:=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$$ in F m$^{-1}$, consistent with the exact SI relation $\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1/c^2$, so that $c^2\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1$ and $\varepsilon_0$ inherits the relative standard uncertainty of $\mu_0$. (b) [Electromagnetic quantities] Charge $q$ carries the coulomb (C); the charge density $\rho$ of the framework's source definition carries C m$^{-3}$ and the current density $J$ carries A m$^{-2}$, so that the four-current components $(c\rho,J)$ carry A m$^{-2}$; the electric field $E$ carries V m$^{-1}$; the magnetic field $B$ carries the tesla (T), where $1\ \mathrm{T}=1\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-1}\,m^{-1}}$; the scalar potential $\varphi$ carries V and the vector potential $A$ carries T m, so that the four-potential components $(\varphi/c,A)$ carry T m; the components of the electromagnetic two-form of the framework's tensor definition carry T; a force carries the newton (N), $1\ \mathrm{N}=1\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}}$

Let the laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$, its spatial Euclidean structure and its units be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] and [[def-em-si-conventions]], and let $k\ge1$. An **electric field of class $C^k$** on the region is a map $E:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ that is of class $C^k$ in the sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]; a **magnetic field of class $C^k$** is a map $B:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ of the same class

Adopt as physical postulates of this framework, on the spacetime and particle model of [[post-em-minkowski-physical-model]] and [[def-em-relativistic-worldlines-frames]] and on the special-relativity particle model [[post-sr-massive-particle-dynamics]]: (i) [Test charge in a prescribed external field] Let $q\in\mathbb R$ be a constant charge parameter ([[def-em-sources]]), $m>0$ an externally supplied rest mass, $x:J\to A$ a future timelike $C^2$ massive worldline with four-velocity $U$, and let $F$ be a prescribed field of [[def-em-electromagnetic-tensor]] that is $C^1$ on a neighbourhood of the graph of $x$ and is generated externally to the particle. Adopt the equation of motion $$m\,\frac{dU}{d\tau}=q\,\Phi(U),$$ where $\Phi$ is the raised-index operator of the field at the event $x(\tau)$, defined by $\eta(\Phi(u),w)=F(w,u)$ ([[lem-em-antisymmetric-tensor-contraction]]); equivalently $m\,dU^\mu/d\tau=q\,F^{\mu\nu}U_\nu$

Let the laboratory region, its inertial chart and the fields and sources be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], [[def-em-fields]] and [[def-em-sources]], with the units of [[def-em-si-conventions]]; fix the ordered basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of the chart and the oriented volume form $\varepsilon$ of [[def-oriented-minkowski-volume-form]], with $\varepsilon_{0123}=+1$ and $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$. (a) [Components] For a field pair $(E,B)$ of class $C^k$, $k\ge1$, define the covariant components of the **electromagnetic two-form** $F$ in the chart by $F_{00}=0$, $F_{0i}:=-E_i/c$, $F_{ij}:=\epsilon_{ijk}B_k$ ($i,j,k\in\{1,2,3\}$) and $F_{ab}:=-F_{ba}$, the index-raised components being $F^{0i}=E_i/c$, $F^{i0}=-E_i/c$ and $F^{ij}=\epsilon_{ijk}B_k$

The particle and light objects of the framework are the following curves and vector fields of the affine Minkowski model ([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]], [[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]), with the physical interpretation of [[post-em-minkowski-physical-model]] and the units of [[def-em-si-conventions]]. (a) [Worldlines] A **worldline** is a regular causal curve $x:J\to A$ in one of the regularity classes of [[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]] ($J$ an order-convex subset of $\mathbb R$ with at least two elements). A **massive worldline** is a $C^k$ future timelike worldline, $k\ge1$, with everywhere nonzero future timelike tangent; a **light ray** is a $C^1$ future null curve with everywhere nonzero future null tangent. Along a null curve the integrand $-\eta(x',x')$ of the proper-time construction ([[def-sr-proper-time]]) vanishes identically, so that construction yields no proper-time parametrization of it, and a light ray is never treated as a massive worldline. A worldline is a curve in spacetime; its reading $r\circ x$ in a named laboratory chart is a coordinate description of it, not an object of another observer. (b) [Four-velocity and four-acceleration] For a massive worldline the four-velocity $U$ and, when it is $C^2$, the four-acceleration $A$ are those of [[def-sr-four-velocity-and-four-acceleration]]; wherever defined they satisfy $\eta(U,U)=-c^2$ and $\eta(U,A)=0$, by [[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]]. (c) [Chart reading] If a massive $C^2$ worldline is described in a laboratory chart of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] by $t\mapsto(ct,r(t))$ on an open interval of laboratory times, then $|r'(t)|<c$ for every $t$, with four-velocity $U=\gamma(c,r')$ and Lorentz factor $\gamma=(1-|r'|^2/c^2)^{-1/2}$, by clause (e) of [[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]]
For $u=(u_x,u_y,u_z)$ and $v=(v_x,v_y,v_z)$ in $\mathbb R^3$, define $u\times v=(u_yv_z-u_zv_y,\,u_zv_x-u_xv_z,\,u_xv_y-u_yv_x)$. This is the right-handed **cross product**
For all $u,v,w\in\mathbb R^3$, the cross product is bilinear and alternating, $\langle u\times v,w\rangle=\det[u\ v\ w]$, and $u\times v$ is orthogonal to both $u$ and $v$

For $u,v\in\mathbb R^3$, $\|u\times v\|_2^2=\det G(u,v)$, and this value is positive exactly when $u$ and $v$ are linearly independent. Equivalently, $$\|u\times v\|_2^2=\|u\|_2^2\|v\|_2^2-\langle u,v\rangle^2.$$

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then: 1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.** $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$ with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$. 2

The class $L^1(\mu)$ is a complex vector space, and the Lebesgue integral is complex-linear on it: $$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$
Let $f,g\in L^1(\mu)$. Then the following are equivalent: 1
If $f\in L^1(\mu)$, then $$\left|\int f\,d\mu\right|\le\int |f|\,d\mu.$$
Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $c\ge0$. 1. If $f\le g$, then $\int f\,d\mu\le\int g\,d\mu$. 2

Throughout this page $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]), in particular an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]]) and a field ([[def-field]]), and $\mathbb{N}$ is the set of natural numbers ([[def-natural-numbers]]) with successor $\sigma(n) = n + 1$ ([[def-nat-addition]]). Let $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ be a sequence of reals, written $a_k$ for $a(k)$. **Finite sums and finite products of $a$ are defined by recursion on the upper index**, which is legitimate because of the recursion theorem ([[thm-recursion]])

Let $a, b, c : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ be sequences of reals, let $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$, and let $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$, with finite sums and finite products as in [[def-finite-sum]]. Then: 1. **Additivity.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n}(a_k + b_k) = \sum_{k<n} a_k + \sum_{k<n} b_k$. 2

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]), let $x \in X$ and let $r \in \mathbb{R}$ with $r > 0$ ([[def-real-order]]). Define $$B(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) < r \,\}, \qquad \bar B(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) \le r \,\}, \qquad S(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) = r \,\}.$$ $B(x,r)$ is the **open ball**, $\bar B(x,r)$ the **closed ball** and $S(x,r)$ the **sphere** of **centre** $x$ and **radius** $r$

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set, and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]], [[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so $$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$ is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$, a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations ([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$. The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number $$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$ the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$ (extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is)

**Clause 1 is about an arbitrary norm; clauses 2 to 4 are about $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ with $n \ge 1$.** 1. **Finite and reverse triangle inequalities.** Let $V$ be a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ and $N$ a norm on it ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]). For every $p \in \mathbb{N}$ and every list $u : p \to V$ ([[def-linear-combination-and-span]]), $$N\Bigl(\sum_{j<p} u_j\Bigr) \;\le\; \sum_{j<p} N(u_j),$$ and for all $u, w \in V$, $$\bigl|N(u) - N(w)\bigr| \;\le\; N(u - w).$$ Now let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ carry the norms of [[def-p-norms-on-rn]] and write $\iota$ for the canonical natural ([[def-canonical-natural]]). 2

derivations.claim: Establish that $F$ and $\tau$ are well defined. For $\lambda_3$-a.e. $y$ either $\rho(y)=0$ or $y\in\overline B_a(0)$, and then $|y|\le a$ by [F11]; the Lipschitz property gives $|E_{\mathrm{ext}}(y)|\le|E_{\mathrm{ext}}(0)|+L|y|\le|E_{\mathrm{ext}}(0)|+La$ and hence $|y\times E_{\mathrm{ext}}(y)|\le|y|\,|E_{\mathrm{ext}}(y)|\le a(|E_{\mathrm{ext}}(0)|+La)$ by [F7] and [F8]. Each component of the integrands is therefore dominated $\lambda_3$-a.e. by a finite constant times $|\rho|\in L^1$, so the componentwise integrals converge absolutely by the triangle and monotonicity rules, and no value of $E_{\mathrm{ext}}$ on a null set matters [F9].

Expand the force and bound its remainder. Write $E_{\mathrm{ext}}(y)=E_{\mathrm{ext}}(0)+\bigl(E_{\mathrm{ext}}(y)-E_{\mathrm{ext}}(0)\bigr)$ and integrate: by finite linearity of the componentwise integral [F9], $F=\bigl(\int\rho\,d\lambda_3\bigr)E_{\mathrm{ext}}(0)+\int\rho(y)\bigl(E_{\mathrm{ext}}(y)-E_{\mathrm{ext}}(0)\bigr)d\lambda_3(y)=QE_{\mathrm{ext}}(0)+R_F$ with $Q$ as in [F1]. If $R_F\ne0$, test against the unit vector $u:=R_F/|R_F|$: $|R_F|=u\cdot R_F=\int\rho(y)\,u\cdot\bigl(E_{\mathrm{ext}}(y)-E_{\mathrm{ext}}(0)\bigr)d\lambda_3(y)\le\int|\rho(y)|\,|E_{\mathrm{ext}}(y)-E_{\mathrm{ext}}(0)|\,d\lambda_3(y)\le L\int|y|\,|\rho(y)|\,d\lambda_3(y)\le La\|\rho\|_1$, using [F8] for $u\cdot v\le|v|$, the Lipschitz hypothesis, the monotonicity rule, and $|y|\le a$ $\lambda_3$-a.e. on the support [F11]; the case $R_F=0$ is trivial. This is the force statement of (a).

Expand the torque and bound its remainder. Since $y\times E_{\mathrm{ext}}(y)=y\times E_{\mathrm{ext}}(0)+y\times\bigl(E_{\mathrm{ext}}(y)-E_{\mathrm{ext}}(0)\bigr)$, finite linearity of the componentwise integral and the bilinearity of the cross product [F7] give $\int\rho(y)\,y\times E_{\mathrm{ext}}(0)\,d\lambda_3(y)=\bigl(\int y\,\rho(y)\,d\lambda_3(y)\bigr)\times E_{\mathrm{ext}}(0)=p\times E_{\mathrm{ext}}(0)$ with $p$ as in [F1], so $\tau=p\times E_{\mathrm{ext}}(0)+R_\tau$ with $R_\tau:=\int\rho(y)\,y\times\bigl(E_{\mathrm{ext}}(y)-E_{\mathrm{ext}}(0)\bigr)d\lambda_3(y)$. For the bound, $|R_\tau|\le\int|\rho(y)|\,|y|\,|E_{\mathrm{ext}}(y)-E_{\mathrm{ext}}(0)|\,d\lambda_3(y)\le L\int|y|^2|\rho|\,d\lambda_3\le La^2\|\rho\|_1$ by [F7], [F9] and [F11]. This is the torque statement of (a).

Specialise to the neutral case (b): if $Q=0$, the leading force term $QE_{\mathrm{ext}}(0)$ vanishes and step 2.1 leaves $F=R_F$ with $|R_F|\le La\|\rho\|_1$, while step 3.1 gives the torque as the ideal-dipole torque plus the stated bound.

Prove the reference-point shift (c). For any $o\in\mathbb R^3$, $(y-o)\times E_{\mathrm{ext}}(y)=y\times E_{\mathrm{ext}}(y)-o\times E_{\mathrm{ext}}(y)$ by bilinearity [F7]; integrating, $o$ is a constant vector and $\int\rho(y)E_{\mathrm{ext}}(y)\,d\lambda_3(y)=F$, so finite linearity [F9] gives $\tau_o=\tau-o\times F$ exactly.

Treat the ideal pair of test charges (d). Under the explicitly adopted finite force assignment $F_k=q_kE_{\mathrm{ext}}(x_k)$, the total force is $F=qE_{\mathrm{ext}}(d/2)-qE_{\mathrm{ext}}(-d/2)=q\bigl(E_{\mathrm{ext}}(d/2)-E_{\mathrm{ext}}(-d/2)\bigr)$, and inserting $\pm E_{\mathrm{ext}}(0)$ gives $F=R_F$ with $R_F=q\bigl[(E_{\mathrm{ext}}(d/2)-E_{\mathrm{ext}}(0))-(E_{\mathrm{ext}}(-d/2)-E_{\mathrm{ext}}(0))\bigr]$ and $|R_F|\le|q|(L|d/2|+L|d/2|)=2|q|La$; the total torque is $\tau=(d/2)\times qE_{\mathrm{ext}}(d/2)+(-d/2)\times(-q)E_{\mathrm{ext}}(-d/2)=q(d/2)\times\bigl(E_{\mathrm{ext}}(d/2)+E_{\mathrm{ext}}(-d/2)\bigr)=q\,d\times E_{\mathrm{ext}}(0)+R_\tau$ with $R_\tau=q(d/2)\times\bigl[(E_{\mathrm{ext}}(d/2)-E_{\mathrm{ext}}(0))+(E_{\mathrm{ext}}(-d/2)-E_{\mathrm{ext}}(0))\bigr]$ and $|R_\tau|\le|q|a\cdot2La=2|q|La^2$, using [F7], the Lipschitz hypothesis and [F10]; the finite-branch moments are $Q=0$ and $p=qd$ by [F1], and no convergence or Lipschitz hypothesis is needed for the bare finite sums themselves. All these sums are finite and choice-free.

Instantiate the exact coupling at an instant of rest, proving (d1). Under the additional hypotheses of (d1) the postulate gives $m\,dU^i/d\tau=q'\Phi(U)^i=q'F^{i\nu}U_\nu$ [F4]; at an instant with $r'=0$ the chart reading of the four-velocity is $U=(c,0,0,0)$ by [F6], so the spatial components $U_j$ vanish, $U_0=\eta_{00}U^0=-c$, and only the term $q'F^{i0}U_0$ survives; with $F^{i0}=-E_i/c$ from [F5] this equals $q'(-E_i/c)(-c)=q'E_i$. Hence the covariant equation reproduces the prescribed assignment $F_k=q_kE_{\mathrm{ext}}(x_k)$ at that instant and nothing more: no $C^1$ tensor or massive worldline is inferred from the continuous datum $E_{\mathrm{ext}}$, and no trajectory or permanent-rest claim is made. In the same way the smooth source branch of the postulate reproduces the continuum density $\rho E$ only when its own stated smoothness and matter hypotheses hold [F4].

Record the scope (e) and close the argument. The prescribed data carry the field units and laboratory conventions of [F2], and the derived member $E=-\nabla\varphi$ would be the fixed-time spatial field object of [F3]; only the prescribed external field acts in the model, the self-field, other fields, mechanical support and back-reaction are excluded by hypothesis, the external field is a datum rather than a solution of any field equation, and clauses (a)-(c) concern the declared source moments of a prescribed distribution without asserting force dynamics, equilibrium or stability; clause (d) is an instantaneous idealisation with mutual interaction and self-fields excluded, and clause (d1) is a conditional instantiation of the exact coupling, so no empirical, radiative or medium-response content is introduced. The volume integrals used the declared Countable Choice through the Lebesgue interface, while the finite-point algebra of (d) is choice-free.

Combine the clauses: step 2.1 and step 3.1 give (a) with the stated bounds, step 4.1 gives (b), step 5.1 gives the exact reference-point shift (c), step 6.1 gives the finite two-charge expansions and their choice-free status (d), and step 7.1 gives the conditional covariant specialization (d1), all under the model assumptions of the statement and with the exclusions of step 8.1, which is (e).

Steps 2.1 and 3.1 show the remainders vanish identically when the Lipschitz constant L is zero; the case R_F=0 is separated in the force bound, and the reference point o=0 is included in step 5.1.

citations.quote: For the Lebesgue branches (a) and (b) assume Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), inherited from the exact measure interface ([[def-countable-choice]]); the finite sums in branch (c) are defined and computed without Choice. Let the laboratory region, its chart, its spatial Euclidean structure and its units be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] and [[def-em-si-conventions]], and let $\delta_{ij}$ be the Kronecker symbol in the $\delta$-orthonormal basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of the frame, with $|y|$ the Euclidean norm of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. This definition assigns **source moments** to a static charge distribution in the fixed-time reading of [[def-em-electrostatic-regime]] (d) and (e). Three branches are declared. (a) [Absolutely continuous branch] Let $a>0$ and let $\rho\in L^1(\mathbb R^3)$ be real ([[def-l-one-of-a-measure]]) and vanish $\lambda_3$-almost everywhere outside the closed ball $\overline B_a(0)=\{y:|y|\le a\}$ ([[def-metric-ball]], [[def-measure-null-set-and-almost-everywhere]]). The **total charge** $Q$, the **dipole moment** $p$, the **degree-$l$ Cartesian moments** $M_{i_1\dots i_l}$ and the **traceless quadrupole** $Q_{ij}$ are $$Q:=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\rho\,d\lambda_3,\qquad p_i:=\int_{\mathbb R^3}y_i\,\rho(y)\,d\lambda_3(y),\qquad M_{i_1\dots i_l}:=\int_{\mathbb R^3}y_{i_1}\cdots y_{i_l}\,\rho(y)\,d\lambda_3(y)\ (l\ge1),$$ $$M^{(0)}:=Q,\qquad M_i:=p_i,\qquad Q_{ij}:=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\bigl(3y_iy_j-|y|^2\delta_{ij}\bigr)\rho(y)\,d\lambda_3(y),$$ with $l\ge1$ and indices in $\{1,2,3\}$; units are C for $Q$, C m for $p$, C m$^l$ for the degree-$l$ Cartesian moment and C m$^2$ for $Q_{ij}$, and all integrals are in the sense of [[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]] and [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]]
Assume Countable Choice and $n\ge2$. For a measurable compactly supported $f$, define $$Nf(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}\Phi(x-y)f(y)\,dy$$ at each $x$ where the integral is absolutely finite

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), inherited from the cited Lebesgue, polar, Newtonian and distribution interfaces ([[def-countable-choice]]). Work in $\mathbb R^3$ with its Euclidean structure ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]], [[def-metric-ball]]) and the constants of [[def-em-si-conventions]], $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}>0$. Let $\Phi$ be the $n=3$ fundamental solution of $-\Delta$ of [[def-laplace-fundamental-solution-with-positive-minus-laplacian-sign]], normalised by $-\Delta T_\Phi=\delta_0$; then $\omega_2=4\pi$ and $$\Phi(z)=\frac{1}{4\pi|z|}\qquad(z\ne0)$$ ([[cor-volume-of-the-unit-n-ball]], [[lem-euclidean-chart-measure-agrees-with-polar-surface-measure]]). Let $Nf$ be the Newtonian potential of [[def-newtonian-potential]]. (a) [Smooth compact sources] Let $\rho:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R$ be of class $C^1$ with compact support contained in $\overline B_R$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]], [[def-metric-ball]]), put $\varphi:=\varepsilon_0^{-1}N\rho$ and $E:=-\nabla\varphi$. Then $\varphi\in C^2(\mathbb R^3)$ ([[thm-newtonian-potential-for-holder-data-is-classical]]), and pointwise on $\mathbb R^3$ $$-\Delta\varphi=\frac{\rho}{\varepsilon_0},\qquad \operatorname{div}E=\frac{\rho}{\varepsilon_0},\qquad \operatorname{curl}E=0$$ with the operators of [[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]] and [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]]. Moreover, with $Q:=\int\rho\,d\lambda_3$, for every $x\in\mathbb R^3$ the absolutely convergent Coulomb integral representation holds, and its far-field bound holds for $|x|>2R$, $$E(x)=\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{x-y}{|x-y|^3}\rho(y)\,d\lambda_3(y)\quad(x\in\mathbb R^3),\qquad |E(x)|\le\frac{\| \rho\|_1}{\pi\varepsilon_0|x|^2}\quad(|x|>2R),$$ and for $|x|>\max(2R,1)$ the potential obeys the decay bound $|\varphi(x)|\le\bigl(|Q|/(4\pi)+R\|\rho\|_1/\pi\bigr)/(\varepsilon_0|x|)$ ([[lem-em-newtonian-far-field-gradient]], [[thm-decay-of-the-newtonian-potential-of-compactly-supported-data]]). The pair $(E,0,\rho,0)$ therefore realises the pure electrostatic regime of [[def-em-electrostatic-regime]] with source $\rho$, and $E$ is the field of the localised Newtonian potential. (b) [Uniqueness with vanishing at infinity] If $\psi\in C^2(\mathbb R^3)$ satisfies $-\Delta\psi=\rho/\varepsilon_0$ pointwise on $\mathbb R^3$ and $\lim_{|x|\to\infty}\psi(x)=0$, then $\psi=\varphi$ ([[thm-weak-maximum-principle-for-the-laplacian]]). In particular, among $C^2$ solutions of the Poisson equation of a compactly supported $C^1$ source decaying at infinity, the localised Newtonian potential is the unique one. (c) [Compactly supported $L^1$ sources] If instead $\rho\in L^1(\mathbb R^3)$ is real, measurable and compactly supported, then $N\rho$ is finite $\lambda_3$-almost everywhere, belongs to $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^3)$, is $C^\infty$ and harmonic off the support of $\rho$, and its regular distribution satisfies $$-\Delta T_{\varepsilon_0^{-1}N\rho}=T_{\rho/\varepsilon_0}\qquad\text{in }\mathcal D'(\mathbb R^3)$$ ([[thm-newtonian-potential-solves-poisson-distributionally]], scaled by $\varepsilon_0^{-1}$; [[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]], [[def-distributional-derivative]])

Adopt the SI system of units for this framework, with the following quantity table and conventions; every symbol is a quantity of this framework and the laboratory structure is that of [[def-em-lab-geometry]]. (a) [Coordinates and constants] $x^0=ct$ and each spatial coordinate $x^i$ carries the metre (m); the time coordinate $t$ carries the second (s); the conversion constant $c>0$ carries m s$^{-1}$ and has the exact SI defining value $c=299\,792\,458\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; the elementary charge $e$ has the exact SI defining value $e=1.602\,176\,634\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$, and this item does not assert that physical charge is quantised; the magnetic constant $\mu_0>0$ carries N A$^{-2}$ and is measured, so no exact numerical value of $\mu_0$ is asserted. The pre-2019 SI fixed the historical nominal $\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}:=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{H\,m^{-1}} =4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-2}}$ exactly; since the revised SI took effect on 20 May 2019, $\mu_0$ is experimentally determined. The SI brochure quotes the nominal $\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}$ as the estimate at the 2019 adoption with relative standard uncertainty $2.3\times10^{-10}$; this is historical estimate and uncertainty context, not an exact equality for the actual $\mu_0$ or a current measured value. The electric constant is defined within the framework by $$\varepsilon_0:=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$$ in F m$^{-1}$, consistent with the exact SI relation $\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1/c^2$, so that $c^2\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1$ and $\varepsilon_0$ inherits the relative standard uncertainty of $\mu_0$

Let $U\cong I\times\Omega$ be the laboratory region of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] with the units, constants and symbols of [[def-em-si-conventions]], let $E:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ and $B:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ be fields of [[def-em-fields]] and let $(\rho,J)$ be source fields of [[def-em-sources]] on $\Omega\times I$, all of class $C^1$ (with every additional derivative appearing below existing and continuous); $\partial_t$ is the partial time derivative at fixed position of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]. (a) [Static regime] The **static (time-independent) electromagnetic regime** on $\Omega\times I$ is the requirement $$\partial_tE=0,\qquad\partial_tB=0,\qquad\partial_t\rho=0,\qquad\partial_tJ=0\qquad\text{on }\Omega\times I.$$ (b) [Pure electrostatics] The **pure electrostatic regime** is the static regime together with $J=0$ and $B=0$ on $\Omega\times I$. (c) [Reduced equations] If the smooth branch of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] holds in the static regime, then the four Maxwell equations reduce to $$\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0,\qquad\operatorname{curl}E=0,\qquad\operatorname{div}B=0,\qquad\operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J$$ pointwise on $\Omega\times I$, with $\operatorname{div}$ and $\operatorname{curl}$ of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] applied at each fixed time; in the pure electrostatic regime the reduction is exactly the pair $\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0$, $\operatorname{curl}E=0$

Let the laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$, its spatial Euclidean structure and its units be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] and [[def-em-si-conventions]], and let $k\ge1$. An **electric field of class $C^k$** on the region is a map $E:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ that is of class $C^k$ in the sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]; a **magnetic field of class $C^k$** is a map $B:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ of the same class

Assume Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), with the exact meaning of [[def-countable-choice]]. Let $P_l$ denote the real vector space of homogeneous polynomials of degree $l$ on $\mathbb R^3$ ([[def-homogeneous-polynomial-and-homogeneous-ideal]], [[def-monomials-multidegree-and-total-degree]]), $H_l=\ker(\Delta:P_l\to P_{l-2})$ with $P_k=\{0\}$ for $k<0$, and let spherical harmonics of degree $l$ be the restrictions of $H_l$ to $S^2$, with unnormalised surface measure $d\Omega$ of total mass $4\pi$ ([[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]], [[lem-euclidean-chart-measure-agrees-with-polar-surface-measure]]). Then $P_l=H_l\oplus|x|^2P_{l-2}$, $\dim H_l=2l+1$, harmonics of distinct degree are orthogonal in $L^2(S^2,d\Omega)$, and the union over $l$ of the spaces of spherical harmonics admits a complete orthonormal basis of $L^2(S^2,d\Omega)$ ([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]]). For any real orthonormal basis $Y_{lm}$, $m=1,\dots,2l+1$, of degree-$l$ harmonics the addition theorem holds:

$$\sum_{m=1}^{2l+1}Y_{lm}(n)Y_{lm}(n')=\frac{2l+1}{4\pi}P_l(n\cdot n'),$$

where $P_l$ is the Legendre polynomial of the convergent zonal kernel lemma ([[lem-em-convergent-legendre-kernel]]). The Laplacian is the Euclidean one ([[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]]). This supplies the harmonic decomposition, orthogonality, completeness and exact addition kernel; it does not assert higher boundary regularity. The purely polynomial decomposition and finite dimension identities use no Choice; the surface/$L^2$/completeness claims retain the stated Countable Choice.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, [[def-countable-choice]]). Let $a>0$ and let $\rho\in L^1(\lambda_3)$ be a real or complex valued Lebesgue integrable function on $\mathbb R^3$ that vanishes $\lambda_3$-almost everywhere outside the closed ball $B_a:=\{y\in\mathbb R^3:\lVert y\rVert_2\le a\}$ ([[def-l-one-of-a-measure]], [[def-metric-ball]]). Put

$$Q:=\int\rho\,d\lambda_3,\qquad p:=\int y\,\rho(y)\,d\lambda_3\in\mathbb C^3,\qquad \lVert\rho\rVert_1:=\int\lvert\rho\rvert\,d\lambda_3,$$

the vector $p$ being defined componentwise; if $\rho$ is real-valued then $Q$ is real and $p\in\mathbb R^3$, while $R(x)$ below is real in that case and complex in general. Then for every $x\in\mathbb R^3$ with $r:=\lVert x\rVert_2\ge2a>0$,

$$\int\frac{\rho(y)}{\lVert x-y\rVert_2}\,d\lambda_3(y)=\frac Qr+\frac{\langle p,x\rangle}{r^3}+R(x),\qquad R(x):=\int_{B_a}\rho(y)\Bigl(\frac1{\lVert x-y\rVert_2}-\frac1r-\frac{\langle x,y\rangle}{r^3}\Bigr)d\lambda_3(y),$$

and the remainder satisfies the explicit bound

$$\lvert R(x)\rvert\le\frac{16\,a^2\,\lVert\rho\rVert_1}{r^3}.$$

Assume Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), with the exact meaning of [[def-countable-choice]]. Let $a>0$ and let $\rho\in L^1(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R)$ vanish outside $\overline B_a(0)$. Use the complete orthonormal basis $\{Y_{lm}\}$ of real spherical harmonics on $S^2$ with unnormalised surface measure $d\sigma$ of total mass $4\pi$ and the addition theorem of [[lem-em-spherical-harmonic-basis-and-addition]], and the Legendre generating kernel and its compact remainder bound from [[lem-em-convergent-legendre-kernel]]. Write $x=rn$, $r=|x|$, $n\in S^2$. Then: (a) **Exterior multipole expansion.** For every $x$ with $|x|>a$, $$\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{\rho(y)}{|x-y|}\,dy=\sum_{l=0}^\infty\sum_{m=1}^{2l+1}\frac{4\pi}{2l+1}\frac{Y_{lm}(n)}{r^{l+1}}\int_{\mathbb R^3}|y|^lY_{lm}(y/|y|)\rho(y)\,dy,$$ the series converging absolutely and uniformly on $\{|x|\ge r_0\}$ for every $r_0>a$, with tail after degree $N$ bounded by $\|\rho\|_1\,a^{N+1}/(r_0^{N+2}(1-a/r_0))$; for every fixed $r>a$, the degree-$l$ term is the $L^2(S^2,d\sigma)$ angular projection of $n\mapsto F_r(n):=\int_{\mathbb R^3}|rn-y|^{-1}\rho(y)\,dy$ onto the degree-$l$ harmonics

Assume Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), with the exact meaning of [[def-countable-choice]]. Let $P_l$ denote the real vector space of homogeneous polynomials of degree $l$ on $\mathbb R^3$ ([[def-homogeneous-polynomial-and-homogeneous-ideal]], [[def-monomials-multidegree-and-total-degree]]), $H_l=\ker(\Delta:P_l\to P_{l-2})$ with $P_k=\{0\}$ for $k<0$, and let spherical harmonics of degree $l$ be the restrictions of $H_l$ to $S^2$, with unnormalised surface measure $d\Omega$ of total mass $4\pi$ ([[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]], [[lem-euclidean-chart-measure-agrees-with-polar-surface-measure]]). Then $P_l=H_l\oplus|x|^2P_{l-2}$, $\dim H_l=2l+1$, harmonics of distinct degree are orthogonal in $L^2(S^2,d\Omega)$, and the union over $l$ of the spaces of spherical harmonics admits a complete orthonormal basis of $L^2(S^2,d\Omega)$ ([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]]). For any real orthonormal basis $Y_{lm}$, $m=1,\dots,2l+1$, of degree-$l$ harmonics the addition theorem holds:

$$\sum_{m=1}^{2l+1}Y_{lm}(n)Y_{lm}(n')=\frac{2l+1}{4\pi}P_l(n\cdot n'),$$

where $P_l$ is the Legendre polynomial of the convergent zonal kernel lemma ([[lem-em-convergent-legendre-kernel]]). The Laplacian is the Euclidean one ([[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]]). This supplies the harmonic decomposition, orthogonality, completeness and exact addition kernel; it does not assert higher boundary regularity. The purely polynomial decomposition and finite dimension identities use no Choice; the surface/$L^2$/completeness claims retain the stated Countable Choice.

For $z\in[-1,1]$ define the real polynomial $P_l(z)=\pi^{-1}\int_0^\pi\bigl[z+i\sqrt{1-z^2}\,\cos\theta\bigr]^l\,d\theta$, $l\in\mathbb N_0$. Then $P_l$ is a real polynomial of degree at most $l$ with $|P_l(z)|\le1$ on $[-1,1]$, $P_l(1)=1$, and for $|q|<1$ the series $\sum_{l\ge0}q^lP_l(z)$ converges absolutely and uniformly on $[-1,1]$ with $$(1-2qz+q^2)^{-1/2}=\sum_{l=0}^{\infty}q^lP_l(z),$$ where the branch is the analytic square root equal to $1$ at $q=0$ ([[def-series-of-real-functions]], [[thm-weierstrass-m-test-for-function-series]])

Let $n\in\mathbb N$, let $f$ have derivatives through order $n$ at $a$, and let $\iota:\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ be the canonical embedding. The **Taylor polynomial of degree at most $n$ about $a$** is $$T_{n,a}f(x):=\sum_{j=0}^{n}\frac{f^{(j)}(a)}{\iota(j!)}(x-a)^j.$$ The **Taylor remainder** is $R_{n,a}f(x):=f(x)-T_{n,a}f(x)$

For $0\le r\le n$, $$(T_{n,a}f)^{(r)}(x)=\sum_{j=r}^{n}\frac{f^{(j)}(a)}{\iota((j-r)!)}(x-a)^{j-r}.$$ Consequently $(T_{n,a}f)^{(r)}(a)=f^{(r)}(a)$, and $R_{n,a}f$ and its derivatives through order $n$ vanish at $a$

Assume Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), with the exact meaning of [[def-countable-choice]]. Let $f\in L^2(S^2,d\Omega)$ with harmonic coefficients $f_{lm}$ in an orthonormal basis of the spherical-harmonic lemma ([[lem-em-spherical-harmonic-basis-and-addition]]), and for $0\le r<1$ set $u(rn)=\sum_{l,m}r^lf_{lm}Y_{lm}(n)$ (the $l=0$ term being the constant value at $r=0$). Then the series and all its derivatives converge uniformly on every closed smaller ball, $u$ is harmonic there ([[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]]), $u(r\,\cdot)\to f$ in $L^2(S^2)$ as $r\uparrow1$, and $u$ is the unique harmonic function on the unit ball with $\sup_{r<1}\|u(r\,\cdot)\|_{L^2}<\infty$ and $L^2$ boundary limit $f$

The class $L^1(\mu)$ is a complex vector space, and the Lebesgue integral is complex-linear on it: $$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$
Let $f,g\in L^1(\mu)$. Then the following are equivalent: 1
If $f\in L^1(\mu)$, then $$\left|\int f\,d\mu\right|\le\int |f|\,d\mu.$$
Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $c\ge0$. 1. If $f\le g$, then $\int f\,d\mu\le\int g\,d\mu$. 2

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]), let $x \in X$ and let $r \in \mathbb{R}$ with $r > 0$ ([[def-real-order]]). Define $$B(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) < r \,\}, \qquad \bar B(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) \le r \,\}, \qquad S(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) = r \,\}.$$ $B(x,r)$ is the **open ball**, $\bar B(x,r)$ the **closed ball** and $S(x,r)$ the **sphere** of **centre** $x$ and **radius** $r$

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set, and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]], [[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so $$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$ is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$, a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations ([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$. The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number $$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$ the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$ (extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is)

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$ be $C^2$ in the sense of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]. Then $\nabla f$ is a $C^1$ field on $U$ by [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]], since each of its components $\partial_if$ has continuous first partial derivatives, so its divergence is defined; the **Laplacian** of $f$ is $$\Delta f:=\operatorname{div}\nabla f=\sum_{i<n}\partial_i\partial_if,$$ with the gradient of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]] and the divergence of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]]
Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open and let $\phi:U\to\mathbb R$ be $C^2$. Then $\nabla\phi$ is a $C^1$ field on $U$ and $$\operatorname{curl}\nabla\phi=0\qquad\text{on }U.$$

Adopt as a physical postulate of this framework the following four equations for the fields of [[def-em-fields]] and the sources of [[def-em-sources]] on the laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$ of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], with $\mu_0>0$, $c>0$, $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ and the SI units of [[def-em-si-conventions]]. (a) [Smooth branch] Let $E,B$ be jointly $C^1$ fields with the additional derivatives required by each equation existing and continuous, and let $\rho,J$ be continuous. Then, with the divergence and curl of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] and the partial derivative $\partial_t$ at fixed position of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], $$\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0,\qquad \operatorname{div}B=0,\qquad \operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB,\qquad \operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J+c^{-2}\partial_tE.$$ (b) [Weak branch] Let instead $E,B$ be locally integrable $\mathbb R^3$-valued fields and $\rho,J$ locally integrable scalar and vector fields on $I\times\Omega$, identified with their regular distributions ([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]], [[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]])

Let $n\in\mathbb N$, and suppose $f$ has derivatives through order $n+1$ on the closed interval between $a$ and $x$, with the usual endpoint continuity. If $|f^{(n+1)}(t)|\le M$ throughout that interval, then
$$|R_{n,a}f(x)|\le \frac{M}{\iota((n+1)!)}|x-a|^{n+1}.$$

derivations.claim: Establish the absolute convergence of the coefficients and the null-singleton convention. On $S^2$ the diagonal addition theorem gives $\sum_{m=1}^{2l+1}Y_{lm}(n)^2=(2l+1)/(4\pi)$ [F8], so $|Y_{lm}(n)|\le((2l+1)/(4\pi))^{1/2}$ for every $n$; for $\lambda_3$-a.e. $y$ with $\rho(y)\ne0$ one has $y\in\overline B_a(0)$ and $|y|\le a$ [F13], so the integrand of $q_{lm}$ is dominated $\lambda_3$-a.e. by $a^l((2l+1)/(4\pi))^{1/2}|\rho|\in L^1$, and $q_{lm}$ is absolutely convergent by [F12]; the definition at $y=0$ affects a null singleton only and changes no integral by [F12].

Prove the exterior expansion and its tail bound (a). By [F3] and [F2] the potential satisfies $\varphi(x)=\varepsilon_0^{-1}N\rho(x)=(4\pi\varepsilon_0)^{-1}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\rho(y)|x-y|^{-1}\,d\lambda_3(y)$ for $r>a$, and [F7] gives $\int\rho(y)|x-y|^{-1}dy=\sum_{l,m}\frac{4\pi}{2l+1}\frac{Y_{lm}(n)}{r^{l+1}}\int|y|^lY_{lm}(y/|y|)\rho\,dy$ with absolute and uniform convergence on $\{|x|\ge r_0\}$ for every $r_0>a$ and the stated tail bound; multiplying the identity and its tail bound by the finite positive constant $(4\pi\varepsilon_0)^{-1}$ [F4] and using scaling [F12] gives (a), with the coefficients exactly the $q_{lm}$ of step 1.1.

Identify the degree-zero and degree-one terms and the exterior remainder, proving the first part of (b). By [F7] the degree-zero and degree-one terms of the parenthesised series are the Coulomb and dipole terms with the explicit remainder bound of [[lem-em-coulomb-dipole-remainder]], namely $Q/r+p\cdot x/r^3$ with $|R_0(x)|\le16a^2\|\rho\|_1/r^3$ for $r\ge2a$; scaling by $(4\pi\varepsilon_0)^{-1}$ as in step 2.1 turns the degree-zero term into $Q/(4\pi\varepsilon_0r)$, the degree-one term into $p\cdot x/(4\pi\varepsilon_0r^3)$, and the remainder bound into the bound of [[pthm-em-electric-dipole-expansion]] (a), which is therefore reproduced.

Identify the degree-two term with the traceless quadrupole, completing (b). Apply the addition theorem [F8] at $l=2$: $\sum_{m=1}^{5}Y_{2m}(n)Y_{2m}(y/|y|)=\frac{5}{4\pi}P_2(n\cdot y/|y|)$, so by finite linearity [F12] $\sum_{m=1}^5Y_{2m}(n)q_{2m}=\frac{5}{4\pi}\int|y|^2P_2(n\cdot y/|y|)\rho(y)\,d\lambda_3(y)$. By [F9] the generating identity $(1-2qz+q^2)^{-1/2}=\sum_lq^lP_l(z)$ holds, and the bound $|P_l(z)|\le1$ in [F9] gives a tail after degree two of modulus at most $|q|^3/(1-|q|)=o(q^2)$ as real $q\to0$. Thus the degree-two partial sum is the Taylor polynomial of the generating function; by [F10] its coefficient of $q^2$ is both $P_2(z)$ and, by the chain rule applied to the power function, $\frac12\frac{d^2}{dq^2}(1-2qz+q^2)^{-1/2}\big|_{q=0}=\frac{3z^2-1}{2}$; hence $P_2(z)=(3z^2-1)/2$ and $|y|^2P_2(n\cdot y/|y|)=(3(n\cdot y)^2-|y|^2)/2$ wherever $y\ne0$. Therefore $\sum_mY_{2m}(n)q_{2m}=\frac{5}{8\pi}\int(3(n\cdot y)^2-|y|^2)\rho\,d\lambda_3=\frac{5}{8\pi}n_iQ_{ij}n_j$ by [F1] and [F12], and the degree-two term of (a) is $\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\cdot\frac{4\pi}{5}\cdot\frac{1}{r^3}\cdot\frac{5}{8\pi}n_iQ_{ij}n_j=\frac{n_iQ_{ij}n_j}{8\pi\varepsilon_0r^3}$.

Prove the regularity and termwise differentiation (c). By [F7] the series may be differentiated termwise to every order with uniform convergence on every compact $K$ with $\inf_K|x|>a$, and the potential is $C^\infty$ on $\{|x|>a\}$; scaling by the constant $(4\pi\varepsilon_0)^{-1}$ preserves termwise differentiation and uniform convergence [F4, F12]. The field $E:=-\nabla\varphi$ of [F6] is therefore the termwise gradient $-\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\sum_{l,m}\frac{4\pi}{2l+1}\nabla_x(Y_{lm}(n)r^{-l-1})q_{lm}$ on $\{|x|>a\}$, with the same uniform convergence on compact subsets.

Record the scope of the exterior clauses (d). Steps 2.1, 3.1, 4.1 and 5.1 used only the real $L^1$ density vanishing $\lambda_3$-a.e. off $\overline B_a(0)$, the region $r>a$ (with the quantitative bounds on $r\ge r_0>a$ and $r\ge2a$), and the framework constants [F4]; no claim on or inside $\overline B_a(0)$, no convergence at $r=a$ and no point-source or empirical assertion was made, and the potential is the fixed-time reading of the static source through [F5].

Prove the ball boundary branch (e). Write $g(un):=\sum_{l,m}u^lf_{lm}Y_{lm}(n)$ for $u\in[0,1)$ and $n\in S^2$ as in [F11] with $u=r/R$ and $n=x/|x|$; then $\varphi_f(rn)=g((r/R)n)$ is smooth and harmonic on $|x|<R$, its series and every derivative converge uniformly on every smaller closed ball because the substitution $x=Rz$ multiplies a derivative of order $\alpha$ by the finite factor $R^{-|\alpha|}$, and the bounds $\sup_{0\le t<1}\|\varphi_f(Rt\,\cdot)\|_2=\sup_{t<1}\|g(t\,\cdot)\|_2\le\|f\|_2$ and $\varphi_f(Rt\,\cdot)\to f$ in $L^2(S^2)$ as $t\uparrow1$ are exactly [F11] in the unit variable; the uniqueness statement carries over because any competitor $v$ on $|x|<R$ gives the competitor $u(z):=v(Rz)$ on the unit ball with the same finite radial $L^2$ bound and boundary limit, so [F11] forces $u=g$ and hence $v=\varphi_f$. For continuous $f$ the Poisson integral of [F11] with $r=|x|/R$ is the displayed formula, and the kernel is positive of mass one. Finally, define $E_f:=-\nabla\varphi_f$, $B:=0$, $\rho:=J:=0$ and time-independent fields on the open ball; then $\varphi_f$ is $C^\infty$, so $E_f$ is a $C^1$ field and $B,\rho,J$ are continuous, and [F14] gives $\operatorname{div}E_f=-\Delta\varphi_f=0$ and $\operatorname{curl}E_f=-\operatorname{curl}\nabla\varphi_f=0$, while $\operatorname{div}B=0$ and $\operatorname{curl}B=0$; all four adopted smooth vacuum Maxwell equations of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] hold pointwise with vanishing sources and time derivatives, so this is a full source-free electrostatic Maxwell model inside the ball. No boundary trace for the exterior density and no derivative boundary regularity for arbitrary $f$ is used or claimed.

Assemble the theorem and close. Step 2.1 gives (a), steps 3.1 and 4.1 give (b), step 5.1 gives (c), step 6.1 records the scope (d), and step 7.1 gives the independent ball boundary branch (e) with its source-free Maxwell completion; the only nonconstructive assumptions are the declared Countable Choice inherited from the Lebesgue, spherical-harmonic and ball-series interfaces, and no exterior trace, singular-source expansion or empirical content is asserted.

boundaries.evidence: Step 2.1 keeps the l=0 term of the exterior series and the corresponding singleton angular sum explicit, so the expansion is not vacuous for a spherically symmetric source, and the coefficient assignment at the origin in step 1.1 is a finite convention.

Step 1.1's coefficient bound is the zero-safe estimate |Y_lm| <= ((2l+1)/(4 pi))^(1/2); steps 2.1 and 4.1 divide only by r>a, by the fixed integers 2l+1, and by 8 pi, while the ball branch of step 7.1 divides by the positive radius R.
Step 1.1 keeps the degree-zero singleton sum over m explicit, and step 4.1 isolates the single degree l=2 with its finite five-term sum over m.

Step 6.1 excludes the boundary r=a and the source support from the exterior claims, and the source-free ball branch of step 7.1 has R>0 with the radial series read at t=0 by the constant degree-zero value.
Step 2.1 treats the exterior endpoint r=r0>a of the uniform-convergence region with the geometric ratio a/r0<1, and step 7.1 handles the boundary limit t->1 in L2 only.

Step 8.1 records the only nonconstructive inputs as the Countable Choice of the Lebesgue, spherical-harmonic and ball-series interfaces; the finite angular sums and the degree identifications are explicit.

boundaries.reason: The exterior expansion, the term identifications and the ball uniqueness are stated as conclusions under hypotheses, not as an equivalence.
No clause is the converse of another: the ball uniqueness is an assertion about a stated harmonic class, not a biconditional requiring two directions.

citations.quote: For the Lebesgue branches (a) and (b) assume Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), inherited from the exact measure interface ([[def-countable-choice]]); the finite sums in branch (c) are defined and computed without Choice. Let the laboratory region, its chart, its spatial Euclidean structure and its units be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] and [[def-em-si-conventions]], and let $\delta_{ij}$ be the Kronecker symbol in the $\delta$-orthonormal basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of the frame, with $|y|$ the Euclidean norm of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. This definition assigns **source moments** to a static charge distribution in the fixed-time reading of [[def-em-electrostatic-regime]] (d) and (e). Three branches are declared. (a) [Absolutely continuous branch] Let $a>0$ and let $\rho\in L^1(\mathbb R^3)$ be real ([[def-l-one-of-a-measure]]) and vanish $\lambda_3$-almost everywhere outside the closed ball $\overline B_a(0)=\{y:|y|\le a\}$ ([[def-metric-ball]], [[def-measure-null-set-and-almost-everywhere]]). The **total charge** $Q$, the **dipole moment** $p$, the **degree-$l$ Cartesian moments** $M_{i_1\dots i_l}$ and the **traceless quadrupole** $Q_{ij}$ are $$Q:=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\rho\,d\lambda_3,\qquad p_i:=\int_{\mathbb R^3}y_i\,\rho(y)\,d\lambda_3(y),\qquad M_{i_1\dots i_l}:=\int_{\mathbb R^3}y_{i_1}\cdots y_{i_l}\,\rho(y)\,d\lambda_3(y)\ (l\ge1),$$ $$M^{(0)}:=Q,\qquad M_i:=p_i,\qquad Q_{ij}:=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\bigl(3y_iy_j-|y|^2\delta_{ij}\bigr)\rho(y)\,d\lambda_3(y),$$ with $l\ge1$ and indices in $\{1,2,3\}$; units are C for $Q$, C m for $p$, C m$^l$ for the degree-$l$ Cartesian moment and C m$^2$ for $Q_{ij}$, and all integrals are in the sense of [[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]] and [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]]. Each integral is absolutely convergent: since $\rho=0$ $\lambda_3$-a.e. off $\overline B_a(0)$, and the maps $y\mapsto y_{i_1}\cdots y_{i_l}$ and $y\mapsto 3y_iy_j-|y|^2\delta_{ij}$ are bounded $\lambda_3$-a.e. on that ball by $a^l$ and by $4a^2$ respectively, the integrands are dominated $\lambda_3$-a.e. by $a^l|\rho|$ and $4a^2|\rho|$, which lie in $L^1$ ([[thm-integral-triangle-inequality]], [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]). The traceless quadrupole is traceless, $$\sum_{i=1}^3Q_{ii}=0,$$ because $\sum_{i=1}^3(3y_i^2-|y|^2)=0$ pointwise, and summing the three integrable functions $3y_i^2\rho-|y|^2\rho$ and applying finite linearity of the integral on $L^1$ ([[thm-linearity-of-the-lebesgue-integral-on-l-one]]) evaluates the sum as the integral of the pointwise-zero function; replacing $\rho$ by an equal $\lambda_3$-a.e. density changes no moment ([[thm-the-lebesgue-integral-respects-almost-everywhere-equality]]). (b) [General locally integrable branch] If instead $\rho\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^3)$ is real and $\int_{\mathbb R^3}|y|^l|\rho(y)|\,d\lambda_3(y)<\infty$ for a given integer $l\ge0$, then the degree-$l$ Cartesian moments of the same formula are absolutely convergent and defined; if the absolute weighted moment $\int_{\mathbb R^3}|y|^L|\rho(y)|\,d\lambda_3(y)$ is finite for some real $L\ge0$, then every integer Cartesian degree $0\le l\le L$ is defined, and in particular $Q=\int\rho\,d\lambda_3$ is absolutely convergent, so that $\rho\in L^1(\mathbb R^3)$ is a conclusion of this branch and not an added hypothesis. Here $\rho$ is restricted to the closed unit ball, where it is integrable by local integrability, and outside it $|y|^l\le|y|^L$; splitting the nonnegative integral over these two measurable sets and applying monotonicity and additivity of the integral gives $\int|y|^l|\rho|\le\int_{\overline B_1(0)}|\rho|+\int_{\{|y|>1\}}|y|^L|\rho|<\infty$ ([[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]], [[def-metric-ball]]). The convention $|y|^0=1$ includes the origin, no compact support and no $L^1$-membership is assumed in this branch, and Cartesian monomials of degree $l$ have modulus at most $|y|^l$, so all lower moments, including $Q$, exist together with the degree-$l$ moment. (c) [Finite system of stationary point charges] Let $N\ge0$, let $x_1,\dots,x_N\in\mathbb R^3$ and let $q_1,\dots,q_N\in\mathbb R$ be charge parameters ([[def-em-sources]] (a)), read as the stationary point charges $q_k\delta_{x_k}$ in the fixed-time reading of [[def-em-electrostatic-regime]] (e); for $N=0$ the lists are empty and every sum below is the empty sum $0$. Define $$Q:=\sum_{k=1}^Nq_k,\qquad p:=\sum_{k=1}^Nq_kx_k,\qquad M_{i_1\dots i_l}:=\sum_{k=1}^Nq_k\,x_{k,i_1}\cdots x_{k,i_l}\ (l\ge1),\qquad M^{(0)}:=Q,$$ $$Q_{ij}:=\sum_{k=1}^Nq_k\bigl(3x_{k,i}x_{k,j}-|x_k|^2\delta_{ij}\bigr),$$ finite sums in the sense of [[def-finite-sum]] ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]]); again $$\sum_{i=1}^3Q_{ii}=0,$$ by finite distributivity

$$ Hence $\delta$ is a symmetric bilinear form on $S$ that is positive definite: $\delta(w,w)\ge0$, with equality exactly for $w=0$ by uniqueness of coordinates in the basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $S$ ([[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]])

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space ([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]), let $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an inertial frame with inertial chart $x:A\to\mathbb R^4$ ([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]), let $c>0$ be the framework's conversion constant, and let $\delta$ be the Euclidean spatial form of that frame on $n^\perp$, $n:=e_0$, with norm $|\cdot|$ and positive spatial orientation ([[def-spatial-euclidean-structure-of-an-inertial-frame]]). Fix a nonempty open interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ ([[def-interval]]) and a nonempty open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$, and put $$U:=\{p\in A:\ \text{there are }t\in I,\ y\in\Omega\text{ with }x^0(p)=ct,\ (x^1,x^2,x^3)(p)=y\}.$$ Then: (a) [Chart restriction] $x(U)=\{(ct,y):t\in I,\ y\in\Omega\}$ and $\Phi:U\to I\times\Omega$, $\Phi(p):=(x^0(p)/c,(x^1,x^2,x^3)(p))$, is a bijection, because the inertial chart $x:A\to\mathbb R^4$ is a bijection and $c>0$; its components are the **laboratory time coordinate** $t(p):=x^0(p)/c$ and the **laboratory position** $r(p):=(x^1(p),x^2(p),x^3(p))$. In the chart coordinates the pair $(t(p),r(p))$ is the reading of the laboratory decomposition of $p$. Writing $r(p)=(r^1(p),r^2(p),r^3(p))\in\mathbb R^3$, the standard basis of $\mathbb R^3$ ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]) labels the three coordinate directions, and the identification $\mathbb R^3\cong n^\perp$ is the linear map $\sum_{i=1}^3 r^i e_i$ into the three-dimensional real vector space $n^\perp$ ([[def-vector-space]], [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]). (b) [Slices and spatial structure] For each $t\in I$ the slice $U_t:=\{p\in U:t(p)=t\}$ is carried bijectively onto $\Omega$ by $r$; the constant vector $n=e_0$ is future unit timelike, and $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is the $\delta$-orthonormal positively oriented basis of $n^\perp$ in which the coordinates of $r$ are expressed

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set, and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]], [[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so $$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$ is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$, a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations ([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$. The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number $$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$ the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$ (extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is)

For the Lebesgue branches (a) and (b) assume Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), inherited from the exact measure interface ([[def-countable-choice]]); the finite sums in branch (c) are defined and computed without Choice. Let the laboratory region, its chart, its spatial Euclidean structure and its units be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] and [[def-em-si-conventions]], and let $\delta_{ij}$ be the Kronecker symbol in the $\delta$-orthonormal basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of the frame, with $|y|$ the Euclidean norm of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. This definition assigns **source moments** to a static charge distribution in the fixed-time reading of [[def-em-electrostatic-regime]] (d) and (e). Three branches are declared. (a) [Absolutely continuous branch] Let $a>0$ and let $\rho\in L^1(\mathbb R^3)$ be real ([[def-l-one-of-a-measure]]) and vanish $\lambda_3$-almost everywhere outside the closed ball $\overline B_a(0)=\{y:|y|\le a\}$ ([[def-metric-ball]], [[def-measure-null-set-and-almost-everywhere]]). The **total charge** $Q$, the **dipole moment** $p$, the **degree-$l$ Cartesian moments** $M_{i_1\dots i_l}$ and the **traceless quadrupole** $Q_{ij}$ are $$Q:=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\rho\,d\lambda_3,\qquad p_i:=\int_{\mathbb R^3}y_i\,\rho(y)\,d\lambda_3(y),\qquad M_{i_1\dots i_l}:=\int_{\mathbb R^3}y_{i_1}\cdots y_{i_l}\,\rho(y)\,d\lambda_3(y)\ (l\ge1),$$ $$M^{(0)}:=Q,\qquad M_i:=p_i,\qquad Q_{ij}:=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\bigl(3y_iy_j-|y|^2\delta_{ij}\bigr)\rho(y)\,d\lambda_3(y),$$ with $l\ge1$ and indices in $\{1,2,3\}$; units are C for $Q$, C m for $p$, C m$^l$ for the degree-$l$ Cartesian moment and C m$^2$ for $Q_{ij}$, and all integrals are in the sense of [[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]] and [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]]. Each integral is absolutely convergent: since $\rho=0$ $\lambda_3$-a.e. off $\overline B_a(0)$, and the maps $y\mapsto y_{i_1}\cdots y_{i_l}$ and $y\mapsto 3y_iy_j-|y|^2\delta_{ij}$ are bounded $\lambda_3$-a.e. on that ball by $a^l$ and by $4a^2$ respectively, the integrands are dominated $\lambda_3$-a.e. by $a^l|\rho|$ and $4a^2|\rho|$, which lie in $L^1$ ([[thm-integral-triangle-inequality]], [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]])

For the density-integral branch assume Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$) through the Lebesgue interface ([[def-countable-choice]]); the finite-point branch of all identities below is choice-free. Let $a>0$ and let $\rho\in L^1(\mathbb R^3)$ be real and vanish $\lambda_3$-a.e. outside $\overline B_a(0)$ ([[def-metric-ball]]), or let $(x_k,q_k)_{k=1}^N$ be a finite system of stationary point charges, with the source moments of [[def-em-electric-moments]] branches (a) and (c) respectively. For $b\in\mathbb R^3$ define the moments **about the reference point $b$** by replacing, in each integrand of [[def-em-electric-moments]] (a) and in each summand of (c), the vector $y$ by $y-b$ (respectively $x_k$ by $x_k-b$): $$Q^{(b)}:=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\rho\,d\lambda_3,\qquad p^{(b)}:=\int_{\mathbb R^3}(y-b)\,\rho(y)\,d\lambda_3(y),$$ $$M^{(b)}_{i_1\dots i_l}:=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\prod_{r=1}^l(y-b)_{i_r}\,\rho(y)\,d\lambda_3(y)\quad(l\ge1),\qquad M^{(b,0)}:=Q^{(b)},$$ $$Q^{(b)}_{ij}:=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\bigl(3(y-b)_i(y-b)_j-|y-b|^2\delta_{ij}\bigr)\rho(y)\,d\lambda_3(y),$$ and analogously with the finite sums $M^{(b)}_{i_1\dots i_l}=\sum_{k=1}^Nq_k\prod_{r=1}^l(x_k-b)_{i_r}$ $(l\ge1)$ and $Q^{(b)}_{ij}=\sum_{k=1}^Nq_k\bigl(3(x_k-b)_i(x_k-b)_j-|x_k-b|^2\delta_{ij}\bigr)$ in the point-charge branch; for $N=0$ the sums are the empty sum $0$. Every displayed integral is absolutely convergent: since $\rho=0$ $\lambda_3$-a.e. off $\overline B_a(0)$, the estimates $|(y-b)_{i_1}\cdots(y-b)_{i_l}|\le(|y|+|b|)^l\le(a+|b|)^l$ and $|3(y-b)_i(y-b)_j-|y-b|^2\delta_{ij}|\le4(|y|+|b|)^2\le4(a+|b|)^2$ hold $\lambda_3$-a.e. on the support, so each integrand is dominated $\lambda_3$-a.e. by a finite constant times $|\rho|\in L^1$ ([[def-em-electric-moments]] (a), [[thm-integral-triangle-inequality]], [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]], [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]). Then: (a) $Q^{(b)}=Q$ for every $b$; (b) $p^{(b)}=p-Qb$, so the dipole moment is independent of the reference point exactly when $Q=0$; (c) for every $l\ge0$, $$M^{(b)}_{i_1\dots i_l}=\sum_{S\subseteq\{1,\dots,l\}}(-1)^{|S|}\Bigl(\prod_{r\in S}b_{i_r}\Bigr)M_{S^{c}},$$ where for a subset $S\subseteq\{1,\dots,l\}$ we write $S^{c}:=\{1,\dots,l\}\setminus S$ and $M_{S^{c}}$ for the Cartesian moment whose index list is $(i_r)_{r\in S^{c}}$ in increasing order of $r$, with the empty index list read as $M_{\emptyset}:=Q$; in particular $$M^{(b)}_{ij}=M_{ij}-b_ip_j-b_jp_i+b_ib_jQ;$$ (d) $Q^{(b)}_{ij}=Q_{ij}-3\bigl(b_ip_j+b_jp_i\bigr)+2(b\cdot p)\delta_{ij}+\bigl(3b_ib_j-|b|^2\delta_{ij}\bigr)Q$; consequently, if $Q=0$ and $p=0$, then $Q^{(b)}_{ij}=Q_{ij}$ for every $b$; (e) [Scope] this is an exact identity between the declared source moments of [[def-em-electric-moments]]; it asserts nothing about fields, forces, dynamics or nature, and the reference point is a choice of coordinate origin, not an operation performed on the source

Throughout this page $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]), in particular an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]]) and a field ([[def-field]]), and $\mathbb{N}$ is the set of natural numbers ([[def-natural-numbers]]) with successor $\sigma(n) = n + 1$ ([[def-nat-addition]]). Let $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ be a sequence of reals, written $a_k$ for $a(k)$. **Finite sums and finite products of $a$ are defined by recursion on the upper index**, which is legitimate because of the recursion theorem ([[thm-recursion]])

Let $a, b, c : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ be sequences of reals, let $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$, and let $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$, with finite sums and finite products as in [[def-finite-sum]]. Then: 1. **Additivity.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n}(a_k + b_k) = \sum_{k<n} a_k + \sum_{k<n} b_k$. 2

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then: 1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.** $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$ with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$. 2

derivations.claim: Compute the total charge and the dipole moment by inserting the four points into the finite sums of [F1]: $Q=q+q+(-q)+(-q)=0$, and $p=q(ae_1)+q(-ae_1)+(-q)(ae_2)+(-q)(-ae_2)=qa(e_1-e_1)+(-q)a(e_2-e_2)=0$, using linearity and the coordinate expansions of [F2], [F3] and [F5].

Show that every odd Cartesian moment vanishes. The configuration is invariant under the central reflection $x\mapsto-x$: the charge $+q$ at $\pm ae_1$ is carried to the charge $+q$ at $\mp ae_1$, and the charge $-q$ at $\pm ae_2$ to the charge $-q$ at $\mp ae_2$, so pairing each point with its image and reindexing the finite sum [F5] gives $M_{i_1\dots i_{2k+1}}=\sum_kq_k\prod_{r=1}^{2k+1}x_{k,i_r}=\sum_kq_k(-x_{k,i_1})\cdots(-x_{k,i_{2k+1}})=-\sum_kq_k\prod_{r}x_{k,i_r}=-M_{i_1\dots i_{2k+1}}$, hence $M_{i_1\dots i_{2k+1}}=0$; the case $k=0$ is the vanishing dipole $p=0$; total charge $Q=0$ was computed separately in step 1.1.

Compute the degree-two Cartesian moment. By [F1] and the coordinates of [F2], $M_{ij}=q(ae_1)_i(ae_1)_j+q(-ae_1)_i(-ae_1)_j-q(ae_2)_i(ae_2)_j-q(-ae_2)_i(-ae_2)_j=qa^2e_{1i}e_{1j}+qa^2e_{1i}e_{1j}-qa^2e_{2i}e_{2j}-qa^2e_{2i}e_{2j}=2qa^2(\delta_{i1}\delta_{j1}-\delta_{i2}\delta_{j2})$, which is $\operatorname{diag}(2qa^2,-2qa^2,0)$ in the frame basis and has vanishing trace $2qa^2(1-1)=0$.

Compute the traceless quadrupole. With [F1], $Q_{ij}=\sum_kq_k(3x_{k,i}x_{k,j}-|x_k|^2\delta_{ij})=3M_{ij}-\delta_{ij}\sum_kq_k|x_k|^2$; each of the four points has $|x_k|=a$ because $|\pm ae_r|^2=a^2\delta(e_r,e_r)=a^2$ by [F2], [F3] and [F6], so $\sum_kq_k|x_k|^2=a^2\bigl(q+q-q-q\bigr)=0$ and $Q_{ij}=3M_{ij}=6qa^2(\delta_{i1}\delta_{j1}-\delta_{i2}\delta_{j2})$, whose trace is $6qa^2(1-1)=0$, in agreement with the general tracelessness of [F4].

Record the reference-point behaviour and the scope. Since $Q=p=0$ by steps 1.1 and 2.1, clause (d) of the origin-shift theorem [F4] gives $Q^{(b)}_{ij}=Q_{ij}$ for every reference point $b$, so the value $\operatorname{diag}(6qa^2,-6qa^2,0)$ is independent of the reference point; no field, force, energy or self-energy of the point charges is computed or claimed, and the computation is a finite source-moment identity for the prescribed stationary charges.

boundaries.evidence: No index set in the computation is empty: the four charges give four summands, and the central-reflection pairing of step 2.1 pairs each charge with a distinct image, so the odd-moment cancellation covers k=0 as well.
Steps 1.1 and 4.1 compute q-dependent finite sums; q=0 gives the zero configuration with all moments vanishing, and no division by q or by a is performed.
Step 3.1 evaluates the degree-two moment as a four-term sum and reads off the single nonvanishing pair of frame components (1,1) and (2,2) directly.
The construction has a>0, so the four points are distinct; no coincident charge is needed, and the case of two coincident charges is outside the fixed configuration of the example.

boundaries.reason: The computation involves no interval or ordered index with boundary terms; only finite sums over four labelled points and finitely many frame components occur.

boundaries.evidence: Step 5.1 records that the whole computation is finite and choice-free; the origin-shift clause used there is a cited theorem, and the item selects nothing from a family of sets.

boundaries.reason: The example states equalities for one configuration of charges; it contains no equivalence.
There is no converse statement attached to the example's equalities.
