Let the laboratory region, its chart, its spatial Euclidean structure and its units be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] and [[def-em-si-conventions]], and let $\delta_{ij}$ be the Kronecker symbol in the $\delta$-orthonormal basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of the frame, with $|y|$ the Euclidean norm of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. This definition assigns **source moments** to a static charge distribution in the fixed-time reading of [[def-em-electrostatic-regime]] (d) and (e). Three branches are declared. (a) [Absolutely continuous branch] Let $a>0$ and let $\rho\in L^1(\mathbb R^3)$ be real ([[def-l-one-of-a-measure]]) and vanish $\lambda_3$-almost everywhere outside the closed ball $\overline B_a(0)=\{y:|y|\le a\}$ ([[def-metric-ball]], [[def-measure-null-set-and-almost-everywhere]]). The **total charge** $Q$, the **dipole moment** $p$, the **degree-$l$ Cartesian moments** $M_{i_1\dots i_l}$ and the **traceless quadrupole** $Q_{ij}$ are $$Q:=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\rho\,d\lambda_3,\qquad p_i:=\int_{\mathbb R^3}y_i\,\rho(y)\,d\lambda_3(y),\qquad M_{i_1\dots i_l}:=\int_{\mathbb R^3}y_{i_1}\cdots y_{i_l}\,\rho(y)\,d\lambda_3(y)\ (l\ge1),$$ $$M^{(0)}:=Q,\qquad M_i:=p_i,\qquad Q_{ij}:=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\bigl(3y_iy_j-|y|^2\delta_{ij}\bigr)\rho(y)\,d\lambda_3(y),$$ with $l\ge1$ and indices in $\{1,2,3\}$; units are C for $Q$, C m for $p$, C m$^l$ for the degree-$l$ Cartesian moment and C m$^2$ for $Q_{ij}$, and all integrals are in the sense of [[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]] and [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]]. Each integral is absolutely convergent: since $\rho=0$ $\lambda_3$-a.e. off $\overline B_a(0)$, and the maps $y\mapsto y_{i_1}\cdots y_{i_l}$ and $y\mapsto 3y_iy_j-|y|^2\delta_{ij}$ are bounded $\lambda_3$-a.e. on that ball by $a^l$ and by $4a^2$ respectively, the integrands are dominated $\lambda_3$-a.e. by $a^l|\rho|$ and $4a^2|\rho|$, which lie in $L^1$ ([[thm-integral-triangle-inequality]], [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]). The traceless quadrupole is traceless, $$\sum_{i=1}^3Q_{ii}=0,$$ because $\sum_{i=1}^3(3y_i^2-|y|^2)=0$ pointwise, and summing the three integrable functions $3y_i^2\rho-|y|^2\rho$ and applying finite linearity of the integral on $L^1$ ([[thm-linearity-of-the-lebesgue-integral-on-l-one]]) evaluates the sum as the integral of the pointwise-zero function; replacing $\rho$ by an equal $\lambda_3$-a.e. density changes no moment ([[thm-the-lebesgue-integral-respects-almost-everywhere-equality]]). (b) [General locally integrable branch] If instead $\rho\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^3)$ is real and $\int_{\mathbb R^3}|y|^l|\rho(y)|\,d\lambda_3(y)<\infty$ for a given integer $l\ge0$, then the degree-$l$ Cartesian moments of the same formula are absolutely convergent and defined; if the absolute weighted moment $\int_{\mathbb R^3}|y|^L|\rho(y)|\,d\lambda_3(y)$ is finite for some real $L\ge0$, then every integer Cartesian degree $0\le l\le L$ is defined, and in particular $Q=\int\rho\,d\lambda_3$ is absolutely convergent, so that $\rho\in L^1(\mathbb R^3)$ is a conclusion of this branch and not an added hypothesis. Here $\rho$ is restricted to the closed unit ball, where it is integrable by local integrability, and outside it $|y|^l\le|y|^L$; splitting the nonnegative integral over these two measurable sets and applying monotonicity and additivity of the integral gives $\int|y|^l|\rho|\le\int_{\overline B_1(0)}|\rho|+\int_{\{|y|>1\}}|y|^L|\rho|<\infty$ ([[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]], [[def-metric-ball]]). The convention $|y|^0=1$ includes the origin, no compact support and no $L^1$-membership is assumed in this branch, and Cartesian monomials of degree $l$ have modulus at most $|y|^l$, so all lower moments, including $Q$, exist together with the degree-$l$ moment. (c) [Finite system of stationary point charges] Let $N\ge0$, let $x_1,\dots,x_N\in\mathbb R^3$ and let $q_1,\dots,q_N\in\mathbb R$ be charge parameters ([[def-em-sources]] (a)), read as the stationary point charges $q_k\delta_{x_k}$ in the fixed-time reading of [[def-em-electrostatic-regime]] (e); for $N=0$ the lists are empty and every sum below is the empty sum $0$. Define $$Q:=\sum_{k=1}^Nq_k,\qquad p:=\sum_{k=1}^Nq_kx_k,\qquad M_{i_1\dots i_l}:=\sum_{k=1}^Nq_k\,x_{k,i_1}\cdots x_{k,i_l}\ (l\ge1),\qquad M^{(0)}:=Q,$$ $$Q_{ij}:=\sum_{k=1}^Nq_k\bigl(3x_{k,i}x_{k,j}-|x_k|^2\delta_{ij}\bigr),$$ finite sums in the sense of [[def-finite-sum]] ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]]); again $$\sum_{i=1}^3Q_{ii}=0,$$ by finite distributivity

Let $U\cong I\times\Omega$ be the laboratory region of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] with the units, constants and symbols of [[def-em-si-conventions]], let $E:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ and $B:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ be fields of [[def-em-fields]] and let $(\rho,J)$ be source fields of [[def-em-sources]] on $\Omega\times I$, all of class $C^1$ (with every additional derivative appearing below existing and continuous); $\partial_t$ is the partial time derivative at fixed position of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]. (a) [Static regime] The **static (time-independent) electromagnetic regime** on $\Omega\times I$ is the requirement $$\partial_tE=0,\qquad\partial_tB=0,\qquad\partial_t\rho=0,\qquad\partial_tJ=0\qquad\text{on }\Omega\times I.$$ (b) [Pure electrostatics] The **pure electrostatic regime** is the static regime together with $J=0$ and $B=0$ on $\Omega\times I$. (c) [Reduced equations] If the smooth branch of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] holds in the static regime, then the four Maxwell equations reduce to $$\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0,\qquad\operatorname{curl}E=0,\qquad\operatorname{div}B=0,\qquad\operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J$$ pointwise on $\Omega\times I$, with $\operatorname{div}$ and $\operatorname{curl}$ of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] applied at each fixed time; in the pure electrostatic regime the reduction is exactly the pair $\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0$, $\operatorname{curl}E=0$. (d) [Fixed-time reading] In the static regime $E,B,\rho,J$ do not depend on $t$, so each is the pullback along $(y,t)\mapsto y$ of a single map on $\Omega$; this fixed-time reading (the spatial field or source) is the object analysed by the electrostatic statements of this page, and no other time dependence is introduced. The equations of (c) are equations between those spatial maps. (e) [Static-to-distributional reading] Let fields $E,B$ and volume densities $\rho,J$ be locally integrable and time independent on $\Omega\times I$, and let $\Omega$ be open. Then, under the $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ convention of the cited measure and distribution interfaces ([[def-countable-choice]]), the weak equations of the solution predicate of [[def-em-weak-sources]](e) for these time-independent objects hold if and only if the four spatial equations $\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0$, $\operatorname{div}B=0$, $\operatorname{curl}E=0$, $\operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J$ hold in $\mathcal D'(\Omega)$; the passage between them is the integration in $t$ of the pairings against $C_c^\infty(I\times\Omega)$ tests, justified by [[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]] after identifying fields and densities with their regular distributions ([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]], [[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]], [[def-distributional-derivative]]). In particular a **stationary point charge** at $x_0\in\Omega$ with charge parameter $q\in\mathbb R$ is the point source of [[def-em-weak-sources]](b) with constant trajectory $z(t)\equiv x_0$, whose pairing is $\psi\mapsto q\int_I\psi(x_0,t)\,dt$ and whose fixed-time reading is the spatial point source $\eta\mapsto q\eta(x_0)$ ([[def-dirac-delta-and-its-derivatives]])

Distributional derivatives satisfy $\partial^\alpha\partial^\beta u=\partial^{\alpha+\beta}u$ and are continuous linear maps on $\mathcal D'(\Omega)$ for both the weak and strong distribution topologies

For a distribution $u\in\mathcal D'(\Omega)$ in the convention of [[def-distribution]] and a multi-index $\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n$, its **distributional derivative** is $$\langle\partial^\alpha u,\varphi\rangle=(-1)^{|\alpha|}\langle u,\partial^\alpha\varphi\rangle\qquad(\varphi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)).$$ The test derivative is a continuous linear endomorphism by [[thm-test-function-operations-are-continuous]]
For $a\in\Omega$, the **Dirac distribution at $a$** is the complex-linear functional $\delta_a(\varphi)=\varphi(a)$ on $\mathcal D(\Omega)$, with the bilinear convention of [[def-distribution]]

For the density-integral branch assume Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$) through the Lebesgue interface ([[def-countable-choice]]); the finite-point branch of all identities below is choice-free. Let $a>0$ and let $\rho\in L^1(\mathbb R^3)$ be real and vanish $\lambda_3$-a.e. outside $\overline B_a(0)$ ([[def-metric-ball]]), or let $(x_k,q_k)_{k=1}^N$ be a finite system of stationary point charges, with the source moments of [[def-em-electric-moments]] branches (a) and (c) respectively. For $b\in\mathbb R^3$ define the moments **about the reference point $b$** by replacing, in each integrand of [[def-em-electric-moments]] (a) and in each summand of (c), the vector $y$ by $y-b$ (respectively $x_k$ by $x_k-b$): $$Q^{(b)}:=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\rho\,d\lambda_3,\qquad p^{(b)}:=\int_{\mathbb R^3}(y-b)\,\rho(y)\,d\lambda_3(y),$$ $$M^{(b)}_{i_1\dots i_l}:=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\prod_{r=1}^l(y-b)_{i_r}\,\rho(y)\,d\lambda_3(y)\quad(l\ge1),\qquad M^{(b,0)}:=Q^{(b)},$$ $$Q^{(b)}_{ij}:=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\bigl(3(y-b)_i(y-b)_j-|y-b|^2\delta_{ij}\bigr)\rho(y)\,d\lambda_3(y),$$ and analogously with the finite sums $M^{(b)}_{i_1\dots i_l}=\sum_{k=1}^Nq_k\prod_{r=1}^l(x_k-b)_{i_r}$ $(l\ge1)$ and $Q^{(b)}_{ij}=\sum_{k=1}^Nq_k\bigl(3(x_k-b)_i(x_k-b)_j-|x_k-b|^2\delta_{ij}\bigr)$ in the point-charge branch; for $N=0$ the sums are the empty sum $0$. Every displayed integral is absolutely convergent: since $\rho=0$ $\lambda_3$-a.e. off $\overline B_a(0)$, the estimates $|(y-b)_{i_1}\cdots(y-b)_{i_l}|\le(|y|+|b|)^l\le(a+|b|)^l$ and $|3(y-b)_i(y-b)_j-|y-b|^2\delta_{ij}|\le4(|y|+|b|)^2\le4(a+|b|)^2$ hold $\lambda_3$-a.e. on the support, so each integrand is dominated $\lambda_3$-a.e. by a finite constant times $|\rho|\in L^1$ ([[def-em-electric-moments]] (a), [[thm-integral-triangle-inequality]], [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]], [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]). Then: (a) $Q^{(b)}=Q$ for every $b$; (b) $p^{(b)}=p-Qb$, so the dipole moment is independent of the reference point exactly when $Q=0$; (c) for every $l\ge0$, $$M^{(b)}_{i_1\dots i_l}=\sum_{S\subseteq\{1,\dots,l\}}(-1)^{|S|}\Bigl(\prod_{r\in S}b_{i_r}\Bigr)M_{S^{c}},$$ where for a subset $S\subseteq\{1,\dots,l\}$ we write $S^{c}:=\{1,\dots,l\}\setminus S$ and $M_{S^{c}}$ for the Cartesian moment whose index list is $(i_r)_{r\in S^{c}}$ in increasing order of $r$, with the empty index list read as $M_{\emptyset}:=Q$; in particular $$M^{(b)}_{ij}=M_{ij}-b_ip_j-b_jp_i+b_ib_jQ;$$ (d) $Q^{(b)}_{ij}=Q_{ij}-3\bigl(b_ip_j+b_jp_i\bigr)+2(b\cdot p)\delta_{ij}+\bigl(3b_ib_j-|b|^2\delta_{ij}\bigr)Q$; consequently, if $Q=0$ and $p=0$, then $Q^{(b)}_{ij}=Q_{ij}$ for every $b$; (e) [Scope] this is an exact identity between the declared source moments of [[def-em-electric-moments]]; it asserts nothing about fields, forces, dynamics or nature, and the reference point is a choice of coordinate origin, not an operation performed on the source
Let $a<b$. Suppose $G:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on $(a,b)$

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and $$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$ ([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$

For $a>0$, the function $x\mapsto a^x$ is continuous on $\mathbb R$ and $$(a^x)'=a^x\log a.$$ For $\alpha\in\mathbb R$, the function $x\mapsto x^\alpha$ is continuous and differentiable on $(0,\infty)$, with $$(x^\alpha)'=\alpha x^{\alpha-1}.$$

**Clause 1 is about an arbitrary norm; clauses 2 to 4 are about $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ with $n \ge 1$.** 1. **Finite and reverse triangle inequalities.** Let $V$ be a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ and $N$ a norm on it ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]). For every $p \in \mathbb{N}$ and every list $u : p \to V$ ([[def-linear-combination-and-span]]), $$N\Bigl(\sum_{j<p} u_j\Bigr) \;\le\; \sum_{j<p} N(u_j),$$ and for all $u, w \in V$, $$\bigl|N(u) - N(w)\bigr| \;\le\; N(u - w).$$ Now let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ carry the norms of [[def-p-norms-on-rn]] and write $\iota$ for the canonical natural ([[def-canonical-natural]]). 2

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]), let $x \in X$ and let $r \in \mathbb{R}$ with $r > 0$ ([[def-real-order]]). Define $$B(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) < r \,\}, \qquad \bar B(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) \le r \,\}, \qquad S(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) = r \,\}.$$ $B(x,r)$ is the **open ball**, $\bar B(x,r)$ the **closed ball** and $S(x,r)$ the **sphere** of **centre** $x$ and **radius** $r$
Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $m,q\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$. A map $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$ is of class $C^k$ when each component is of class $C^k$
If $f\in L^1(\mu)$, then $$\left|\int f\,d\mu\right|\le\int |f|\,d\mu.$$
Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $c\ge0$. 1. If $f\le g$, then $\int f\,d\mu\le\int g\,d\mu$. 2

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then: 1. **Nonnegativity.** If $f(x) \ge 0$ for every $x \in [a,b]$ then $\int_a^b f \ge 0$. 2. **Monotonicity.** If $f(x) \le g(x)$ for every $x \in [a,b]$ then $$\int_a^b f \;\le\; \int_a^b g .$$ 3
Let $f,g\in L^1(\mu)$. Then the following are equivalent: 1

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set, and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]], [[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so $$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$ is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$, a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations ([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$. The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number $$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$ the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$ (extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is)

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then: 1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.** $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$ with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$. 2

Throughout this page $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]), in particular an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]]) and a field ([[def-field]]), and $\mathbb{N}$ is the set of natural numbers ([[def-natural-numbers]]) with successor $\sigma(n) = n + 1$ ([[def-nat-addition]]). Let $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ be a sequence of reals, written $a_k$ for $a(k)$. **Finite sums and finite products of $a$ are defined by recursion on the upper index**, which is legitimate because of the recursion theorem ([[thm-recursion]])

Let $a, b, c : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ be sequences of reals, let $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$, and let $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$, with finite sums and finite products as in [[def-finite-sum]]. Then: 1. **Additivity.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n}(a_k + b_k) = \sum_{k<n} a_k + \sum_{k<n} b_k$. 2

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space ([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]), let $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an inertial frame with inertial chart $x:A\to\mathbb R^4$ ([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]), let $c>0$ be the framework's conversion constant, and let $\delta$ be the Euclidean spatial form of that frame on $n^\perp$, $n:=e_0$, with norm $|\cdot|$ and positive spatial orientation ([[def-spatial-euclidean-structure-of-an-inertial-frame]]). Fix a nonempty open interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ ([[def-interval]]) and a nonempty open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$, and put $$U:=\{p\in A:\ \text{there are }t\in I,\ y\in\Omega\text{ with }x^0(p)=ct,\ (x^1,x^2,x^3)(p)=y\}.$$ Then: (a) [Chart restriction] $x(U)=\{(ct,y):t\in I,\ y\in\Omega\}$ and $\Phi:U\to I\times\Omega$, $\Phi(p):=(x^0(p)/c,(x^1,x^2,x^3)(p))$, is a bijection, because the inertial chart $x:A\to\mathbb R^4$ is a bijection and $c>0$; its components are the **laboratory time coordinate** $t(p):=x^0(p)/c$ and the **laboratory position** $r(p):=(x^1(p),x^2(p),x^3(p))$. In the chart coordinates the pair $(t(p),r(p))$ is the reading of the laboratory decomposition of $p$. Writing $r(p)=(r^1(p),r^2(p),r^3(p))\in\mathbb R^3$, the standard basis of $\mathbb R^3$ ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]) labels the three coordinate directions, and the identification $\mathbb R^3\cong n^\perp$ is the linear map $\sum_{i=1}^3 r^i e_i$ into the three-dimensional real vector space $n^\perp$ ([[def-vector-space]], [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]). (b) [Slices and spatial structure] For each $t\in I$ the slice $U_t:=\{p\in U:t(p)=t\}$ is carried bijectively onto $\Omega$ by $r$; the constant vector $n=e_0$ is future unit timelike, and $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is the $\delta$-orthonormal positively oriented basis of $n^\perp$ in which the coordinates of $r$ are expressed

Adopt the SI system of units for this framework, with the following quantity table and conventions; every symbol is a quantity of this framework and the laboratory structure is that of [[def-em-lab-geometry]]. (a) [Coordinates and constants] $x^0=ct$ and each spatial coordinate $x^i$ carries the metre (m); the time coordinate $t$ carries the second (s); the conversion constant $c>0$ carries m s$^{-1}$ and has the exact SI defining value $c=299\,792\,458\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; the elementary charge $e$ has the exact SI defining value $e=1.602\,176\,634\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$, and this item does not assert that physical charge is quantised; the magnetic constant $\mu_0>0$ carries N A$^{-2}$ and is measured, so no exact numerical value of $\mu_0$ is asserted. The pre-2019 SI fixed the historical nominal $\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}:=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{H\,m^{-1}} =4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-2}}$ exactly; since the revised SI took effect on 20 May 2019, $\mu_0$ is experimentally determined. The SI brochure quotes the nominal $\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}$ as the estimate at the 2019 adoption with relative standard uncertainty $2.3\times10^{-10}$; this is historical estimate and uncertainty context, not an exact equality for the actual $\mu_0$ or a current measured value. The electric constant is defined within the framework by $$\varepsilon_0:=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$$ in F m$^{-1}$, consistent with the exact SI relation $\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1/c^2$, so that $c^2\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1$ and $\varepsilon_0$ inherits the relative standard uncertainty of $\mu_0$

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following statement. > For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by > $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that > $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$

For a measure $\mu$, write $$L^1(\mu):=\{f:X\to\mathbb C:\ f \text{ is integrable}\}.$$ Here **integrable** is the notion introduced in [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]]

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable, and let $E\in\mathcal A$. Since [[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]] implies that $f\chi_E$ is measurable, define the **integral of $f$ over $E$** by $$\int_E f\,d\mu:=\int f\chi_E\,d\mu,$$ where the integral on the right is the nonnegative Lebesgue integral of [[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]]

Let $f:X\to\mathbb R$ be measurable. Its positive and negative parts are $$f^+:=\max\{f,0\},\qquad f^-:=\max\{-f,0\};$$ they are measurable by [[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]] and satisfy $f=f^+-f^-$ and $|f|=f^++f^-$. The **Lebesgue integral of a real measurable function** is defined whenever at most one of $\int f^+\,d\mu$ and $\int f^-\,d\mu$ is $+\infty$, in which case $$\int f\,d\mu:=\int f^+\,d\mu-\int f^-\,d\mu.$$ The function is **integrable** when both integrals are finite, equivalently when $\int|f|\,d\mu<+\infty$

derivations.claim: Prove (a). Each summand is the point-charge object of [F1] with $x_0=\pm d/2$ and charge $\pm q$; each is locally integrable and $C^\infty$ off its pole, so the sum $\varphi$ is locally integrable and $C^\infty$ off $\{d/2,-d/2\}$, with $E=-\nabla\varphi=E_{+q}+E_{-q}$ there. The regular distribution of a locally integrable function is unaffected by changing it on the two-point null set [F12], and distributional differentiation is linear [F4], so adding the two identities of [F1] in $\mathcal D'(\mathbb R^3)$ and using [F5] gives $\operatorname{div}E=\bigl(q\delta_{d/2}-q\delta_{-d/2}\bigr)/\varepsilon_0$ and $\operatorname{curl}E=0$; the dictionary identifying this spatial equation with the fixed-time reading of the source is [F3], and $E$ is the field object defined in [[def-em-fields]]. The chart, its origin and the constant $\varepsilon_0$ are those of [F15], and the distributional and Lebesgue readings used here carry the declared Countable Choice and measure interface of [F16].

Prove the moment and quadrupole clauses of (b). Insert the two points into the finite sums of [F2]: $Q=q+(-q)=0$ and $p=q(d/2)+(-q)(-d/2)=qd$; for every $l\ge1$, $M_{i_1\dots i_l}=q\prod_{r=1}^l(d/2)_{i_r}+(-q)\prod_{r=1}^l(-d/2)_{i_r}=q\bigl(1-(-1)^l\bigr)\prod_{r=1}^l(d/2)_{i_r}$, which vanishes for even $l$ and equals $2q\prod_{r=1}^l(d/2)_{i_r}$ for odd $l$, in particular $M_{i_1\dots i_{2k+1}}=2q(d/2)_{i_1}\cdots(d/2)_{i_{2k+1}}$ and $M_{ij}=0$. Each point has $|x_k|=\bigl|\pm d/2\bigr|=\tfrac12|d|=a$ by the norm formula of [F13], and $\sum_kq_k|x_k|^2=a^2\bigl(q+(-q)\bigr)=0$, so the second formula of [F2] gives $Q_{ij}=3M_{ij}-\delta_{ij}\sum_kq_k|x_k|^2=0$; the identities used only finite distributivity [F14].

Prove the reference-point clause of (e). With $Q=0$ the transformation of [F6] reads $Q^{(b)}_{ij}=Q_{ij}-3(b_ip_j+b_jp_i)+2(b\cdot p)\delta_{ij}$, and substituting $Q_{ij}=0$ and $p=qd$ from step 2.1 gives $Q^{(b)}_{ij}=-3(b_ip_j+b_jp_i)+2(b\cdot p)\delta_{ij}$, which vanishes at $b=0$ and generally does not vanish at other reference points; if $q=0$ then all moments and the potential vanish, and the invariance special case $Q=p=0$ holds.

Establish the far-field identity and bound, proving (c). Fix $y\in\{d/2,-d/2\}$ and $x$ with $r=|x|\ge2a$, and put $h_y(s):=|x-sy|^{-1}$ for $s\in[0,1]$. For all such $s$ the reverse triangle inequality gives $|x-sy|\ge r-s|y|\ge r-a\ge r/2>0$ [F9], so $h_y$ is $C^\infty$ on $[0,1]$ with $h_y(0)=1/r$; the chain rule and the derivative of the power map give $h_y'(s)=\frac{(x-sy)\cdot y}{|x-sy|^3}$ and $h_y''(s)=-\frac{|y|^2}{|x-sy|^3}+3\frac{((x-sy)\cdot y)^2}{|x-sy|^5}$, so $|h_y''(s)|\le\frac{4|y|^2}{|x-sy|^3}\le\frac{32|y|^2}{r^3}$ by [F13] [F8, F10]. The function $s\mapsto(1-s)h_y'(s)+h_y(s)$ has derivative $(1-s)h_y''(s)$, so [F7] gives $h_y(1)-h_y(0)-h_y'(0)=\int_0^1(1-t)h_y''(t)\,dt$, whose modulus is at most $\frac{32|y|^2}{r^3}\cdot\frac12=\frac{16|y|^2}{r^3}$ by [F11]; hence $h_y(1)=\frac1r+\frac{x\cdot y}{r^3}+R_y(x)$ with $|R_y(x)|\le\frac{16|y|^2}{r^3}=\frac{16a^2}{r^3}$.

Substitute the two kernels into $\varphi$, completing (c). Since $|y|=a$ for both points and $q+(-q)=0$ for the constant terms and $q(d/2)\cdot x+(-q)(-d/2)\cdot x=q\,d\cdot x=p\cdot x$ for the linear terms, step 4.1 gives $\varphi(x)=\frac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\bigl(h_{d/2}(1)-h_{-d/2}(1)\bigr)=\frac{p\cdot x}{4\pi\varepsilon_0r^3}+R(x)$ with $R=\frac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\bigl(R_{d/2}(x)-R_{-d/2}(x)\bigr)$, so $|R(x)|\le\frac{|q|(16a^2+16a^2)}{4\pi\varepsilon_0r^3}=\frac{32|q|a^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0r^3}=\frac{8|q|a^2}{\pi\varepsilon_0r^3}$.

Draw the comparison (d) and the scope (e). The theorem of [[pthm-em-electric-dipole-expansion]] assumes an $L^1$ density vanishing a.e. off a ball and therefore does not apply to the singular pair; the identity and bound just proved for the two kernels are the direct twice-fundamental-theorem computation of step 4.1, and substituting the total variation $2|q|$ into that theorem's remainder bound $16a^2\|\rho\|_1/(4\pi\varepsilon_0r^3)$ would give exactly $\frac{8|q|a^2}{\pi\varepsilon_0r^3}$, in agreement with step 5.1; no self-energy, self-force, dynamics, bound-state, stability or empirical assertion is made for the singular pair, and the vanishing of the quadrupole holds at the symmetric origin only, with the general reference point governed by step 3.1, which is (e).

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$ be $C^2$ in the sense of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]. Then $\nabla f$ is a $C^1$ field on $U$ by [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]], since each of its components $\partial_if$ has continuous first partial derivatives, so its divergence is defined; the **Laplacian** of $f$ is

$$\Delta f:=\operatorname{div}\nabla f=\sum_{i<n}\partial_i\partial_if,$$

with the gradient of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]] and the divergence of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]]. A $C^2$ function with $\Delta f=0$ on $U$ is called **harmonic** on $U$.

For a $C^2$ map $F=(F_0,\ldots,F_{q-1}):U\to\mathbb R^q$, whose components are $C^2$ by [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]], $\Delta F$ is the field whose $i$th coordinate is $\Delta F_i$. In the three-coordinate naming of this page, $\Delta f=\partial_x\partial_xf+\partial_y\partial_yf+\partial_z\partial_zf$ and $\Delta F=(\Delta F_x,\Delta F_y,\Delta F_z)$.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $F=(F_0,\ldots,F_{n-1}):U\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^1$ in the componentwise Euclidean sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]. Then the **divergence** of $F$ is $\operatorname{div}F:=\sum_{i<n}\partial_iF_i$, the function $U\to\mathbb R$ whose value at $p$ is $\sum_{i<n}\partial_iF_i(p)$. The partial derivatives are those of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], and the sum is the finite sum used throughout [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Since each $\partial_iF_i$ is continuous on $U$, so is $\operatorname{div}F$.

Now let $n=3$ and let $F:U\to\mathbb R^3$ be $C^1$ on an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$. Following [[def-cross-product-in-r3]], write the three coordinates of a point and of a vector as $x,y,z$ rather than $0,1,2$, so that $F=(F_x,F_y,F_z)$ means $F=(F_0,F_1,F_2)$ and $\partial_x,\partial_y,\partial_z$ are $\partial_0,\partial_1,\partial_2$. With that naming, the **curl** of $F$ is $\operatorname{curl}F:=(\partial_yF_z-\partial_zF_y,\ \partial_zF_x-\partial_xF_z,\ \partial_xF_y-\partial_yF_x)$, a map $U\to\mathbb R^3$ each of whose coordinates is continuous on $U$. In this naming the divergence reads $\operatorname{div}F=\partial_xF_x+\partial_yF_y+\partial_zF_z$.

Both operators are defined pointwise from the first partial derivatives of the components, so no differentiability of $F$ beyond $C^1$ is used and no orientation or metric structure enters beyond the standard coordinates of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]. For a $C^1$ scalar function $f$ on $U$, the gradient $\nabla f=(\partial_0f,\ldots,\partial_{n-1}f)$ is that of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]; in the three-coordinate naming, $\nabla f=(\partial_xf,\partial_yf,\partial_zf)$.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, $a\in U$, $v\in\mathbb R^m$, and $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. If the line map $t\mapsto f(a+tv)$ is defined near $0$, its derivative at $0$ is the **directional derivative**

$$D_vf(a):=\lim_{t\to0}\frac{f(a+tv)-f(a)}{t}.$$

For a standard basis vector $e_j$ ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), $D_{e_j}f(a)$ is the **$j$th partial derivative**, written $\partial_jf(a)$. These are ordinary vector-valued one-variable derivatives in the sense of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]].

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open and let $F:U\to\mathbb R^3$ be $C^2$. Then $\operatorname{curl}F$ is a $C^1$ field on $U$ and

$$\operatorname{div}(\operatorname{curl}F)=0\qquad\text{on }U.$$

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open and let $F:U\to\mathbb R^3$ be $C^2$. Then $\operatorname{curl}\operatorname{curl}F$, $\nabla\operatorname{div}F$ and $\Delta F$ are all defined on $U$ and

$$\operatorname{curl}\operatorname{curl}F=\nabla\operatorname{div}F-\Delta F.$$

Here $\Delta F$ is the componentwise Laplacian of [[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]].

For the Lebesgue/surface/distributional source and admissibility branches (c)-(d), assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). The smooth formulation in (a) and the smooth conserved-current predicate in (b) do not themselves use Choice. Let the laboratory region and its chart, the field and source objects and the units be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], [[def-em-fields]], [[def-em-sources]] and [[def-em-si-conventions]], and fix $\mu_0>0$, $c>0$, $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$.

**(a) [Steady-current regime].** A steady-current (magnetostatic) configuration on $\Omega\times I$ consists of a field pair $E,B:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ and source fields $\rho:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R$, $J:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ that are independent of $t$ and satisfy the smooth branch of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] with the operators of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] and [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]. For such a configuration the formal distributional branch of [[pthm-em-charge-continuity]] gives $\operatorname{div}J=0$ distributionally; this is pointwise when $J$ is $C^1$. In the jointly $C^2$ field/$C^1$ source branch its classical proof applies directly. The locally integrable distributional reading here inherits Countable Choice, whereas the stated classical $C^2/C^1$ compatibility calculation is choice-free, and the four adopted equations are equivalent to the electrostatic pair and the magnetostatic pair
$$\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0,\qquad \operatorname{curl}E=0,\qquad \operatorname{div}B=0,\qquad \operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J .$$

**(b) [Compact smooth current class].** The compact smooth current class of this framework consists of the currents $J\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ with $\operatorname{div}J=0$, extended by zero to $\mathbb R^3$. A magnetostatic field of such a current is a field $B$ of class $C^1$ on $\mathbb R^3$ satisfying $\operatorname{div}B=0$ and $\operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J$ on $\mathbb R^3$ with the extended $J$. This is the hypothesis class of the vector-potential, Biot-Savart and dipole theorems of this page; this definition asserts neither existence nor uniqueness of $B$ in the class.

**(c) [Ideal source objects].** Define three ideal current source objects outside the compact class, together with the data selecting their fields.

**(c1) [Closed thin loop].** For a closed embedded $C^2$ curve $\gamma:\mathbb R/L\mathbb Z\to\mathbb R^3$ with $|\gamma'|\equiv1$ ($L>0$) and $I\in\mathbb R$, the ideal loop current is the distribution
$$\langle J_\gamma,\psi\rangle:=I\int_0^L\gamma'(s)\cdot\psi(\gamma(s))\,ds,\qquad \psi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3),$$
with $\rho_\gamma:=0$.

**(c2) [Infinite straight wire].** For $\gamma(s)=(0,0,s)$, $s\in\mathbb R$, and $I\in\mathbb R$, the ideal wire current is
$$\langle J_{\rm w},\psi\rangle:=I\int_{\mathbb R}\psi_3(0,0,s)\,ds,$$
with $\rho_{\rm w}:=0$.

**(c3) [Infinite cylindrical sheet].** For $a>0$, $S=\{\rho=a\}$, $\rho=\sqrt{x_1^2+x_2^2}$, and $K\in\mathbb R$, the ideal solenoid sheet current is
$$\langle J_S,\psi\rangle:=K\int_S e_\varphi\cdot\psi\,dS$$
([[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]], read on compact cylinder segments), with $\rho_S:=0$. All three pairings are finite because $\psi$ has compact support.

**(c4) [Admissibility].** A field $B$ is admitted for one of these declared models when: $B$ is locally integrable on $\mathbb R^3$ (hence a distribution by [[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]], [[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]]) and $C^1$ off the support of the current; $\operatorname{div}B=0$ and $\operatorname{curl}B=0$ hold pointwise off that support; the distributional identities $\operatorname{div}B=0$ and $\operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J$ hold against every scalar divergence test $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$ and vector curl test $\psi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$ in the sense of [[def-distributional-derivative]]; $B$ has the model's declared symmetry (invariance under translations along and rotations about the axis in (c2) and (c3); no symmetry is required in (c1)); and $B$ obeys the decay requirement: $|B(x)|\to0$ as $|x|\to\infty$ in (c1), and in (c2), (c3) the supremum of $|B|$ over every compact set of cross-sectional parameters tends to $0$ as the transverse radius $\rho\to\infty$. The companion examples exhibit and verify the fields of the two axisymmetric models in this class; the definition itself asserts no existence, uniqueness, finite energy or limiting relation for the declared models, and no compact-class theorem of this page applies to them.

**(d) [Scope].** This is a model restriction: the steady-current regime for compact smooth currents, and three explicitly declared ideal noncompact or singular models. It excludes point charges, weaker-regularity volume sources, moving sheets, normal sheet currents and any claim of empirical exactness; the equations in (c4) define a mathematical admissibility predicate; its physical adoption for these source objects is a separate postulate, and no product of distributions is formed.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), with the exact meaning of [[def-countable-choice]]. Let $\varepsilon_0>0$ be any scalar parameter and let $f\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R)$ and let $$Nf(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{f(y)}{4\pi|x-y|}\,dy .$$ Then $Nf\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$, $-\Delta Nf=f$ pointwise, and for every multi-index $\alpha$ the spatial derivative satisfies $D^\alpha Nf=N(D^\alpha f)$. In particular, for smooth compactly supported $\rho$ the field $E=-\varepsilon_0^{-1}\nabla N\rho$ is smooth. The statement is about the explicit integral transform of compactly supported smooth data and does not assume smoothness of the kernel at the pole; the distributional identity $-\Delta Nf=f$ is the one supplied by the Newtonian-potential theorem ([[thm-newtonian-potential-solves-poisson-distributionally]]), upgraded here from a distributional to a pointwise identity for smooth data.

Adopt as a physical postulate of this framework the following four equations for
the fields of [[def-em-fields]] and the sources of [[def-em-sources]] on the
laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$ of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], with
$\mu_0>0$, $c>0$, $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ and the SI units of
[[def-em-si-conventions]].

(a) [Smooth branch] Let $E,B$ be jointly $C^1$ fields with the additional
derivatives required by each equation existing and continuous, and let
$\rho,J$ be continuous. Then, with the divergence and curl of
[[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] and the partial derivative
$\partial_t$ at fixed position of
[[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]],

$$\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0,\qquad \operatorname{div}B=0,\qquad \operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB,\qquad \operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J+c^{-2}\partial_tE.$$

(b) [Weak branch] Let instead $E,B$ be locally integrable $\mathbb R^3$-valued
fields and $\rho,J$ locally integrable scalar and vector fields on
$I\times\Omega$, identified with their regular distributions
([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]],
[[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]]). Let
$\operatorname{div}$, $\operatorname{curl}$ and $\partial_t$ act as
distributional derivatives, componentwise, and let $\psi$ range over
$C_c^\infty(I\times\Omega)$ ([[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]).
Then the same four identities hold in the sense of [[def-distribution]]: the
pairings

$$\langle\operatorname{div}E-\rho/\varepsilon_0,\psi\rangle,\qquad \langle\operatorname{div}B,\psi\rangle,\qquad \langle\operatorname{curl}E+\partial_tB,\psi\rangle,\qquad \langle\operatorname{curl}B-\mu_0J-c^{-2}\partial_tE,\psi\rangle$$

all vanish for every such $\psi$, all derivatives being distributional
derivatives ([[def-distributional-derivative]]).

(c) [Scope] The postulate contains no magnetic charge: $\operatorname{div}B=0$
and no magnetic-source term appears in $\operatorname{curl}E$. Sources that
are not locally integrable functions (point or sheet sources) are covered by
neither branch and require their own definition. The equations are adopted
classical vacuum physics in the named inertial chart; they are not deduced from
charge conservation, from empirical agreement or from the special-relativity
postulates, and this item by itself asserts no covariance under changes of
inertial frame.

derivations.claim: For each $i$ the datum $J_i$ is smooth and compactly supported, so [F1] gives $A_i=\mu_0N(J_i)\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$, the derivative identity $D^\alpha A_i=\mu_0N(D^\alpha J_i)$ for every multi-index $\alpha$, and $-\Delta A_i=\mu_0J_i$ pointwise on $\mathbb R^3$; since all components are smooth, $A\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$ by [F2], and $-\Delta A=\mu_0J$ holds pointwise componentwise. This is (a).

Taking $\alpha=e_i$ in the derivative identity of step 1.1 and summing, $\operatorname{div}A=\sum_i\partial_iA_i=\mu_0\sum_iN(\partial_iJ_i)$; $N$ is componentwise linear by finite additivity of the integral over the compactly supported data, so this equals $\mu_0N(\sum_i\partial_iJ_i)=\mu_0N(\operatorname{div}J)$ pointwise, and $\operatorname{div}J=0$ gives $\operatorname{div}A=0$ on $\mathbb R^3$. This is (b), and the hypothesis $\operatorname{div}J=0$ is used in no other step.

Since $A$ is $C^\infty$, the field $B:=\operatorname{curl}A$ is $C^\infty$ by [F2]. Then $\operatorname{div}B=\operatorname{div}\operatorname{curl}A=0$ by [F3], and $\operatorname{curl}B=\operatorname{curl}\operatorname{curl}A=\nabla(\operatorname{div}A)-\Delta A$ by [F4]; substituting step 2.1 and step 1.1 gives $\operatorname{curl}B=0-(-\mu_0J)=\mu_0J$. Hence the magnetostatic pair of [F5] holds pointwise on $\mathbb R^3$.

Read step 3.1 inside the framework: [F5] identifies the pair $\operatorname{div}B=0$, $\operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J$ with the time-independent reduction of the adopted equations, and the smooth branch of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]](a) then holds for the fields $E:=0$, $\rho:=0$ on $\Omega\times I$ and the time-independent $B,J$ restricted to $\Omega\times I$: indeed $\operatorname{div}E=0=\rho/\varepsilon_0$, $\operatorname{curl}E=0$ and $\partial_tB=0$ give $\operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB$, $\operatorname{div}B=0$, and $\partial_tE=0$ with $\operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J$ gives $\operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J+c^{-2}\partial_tE$. More generally a compatible steady electrostatic pair satisfying $\operatorname{curl}E=0$ and $\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0$ may be combined with $B,J$; no existence theorem for such a pair is asserted here.

Clauses (a)-(d) are steps 1.1, 2.1, 3.1, 4.1 together with the scope statement: $A$ is a vector potential for $B$ in the Coulomb gauge, the gauge condition $\operatorname{div}A=0$ is a construction choice, and no uniqueness of $A$, no uniqueness of $B$ and no statement for the ideal noncompact models of [[def-em-steady-current-regime]](c) is claimed. Countable Choice is used only through the Newtonian-potential supplier [F1] and the measure interfaces it inherits [F6]; no stronger choice principle occurs, and the vector identities of [F3], [F4] are choice-free.

boundaries.evidence: For $J=0$ the construction of step 1.1 gives $A=0$ and the field $B=0$, for which the pair $\operatorname{div}B=0$, $\operatorname{curl}B=0$ holds; no nonempty source is required by the Statement.
The zero-current case of step 1.1 and step 3.1 reduces the magnetostatic pair to $\mu_0J=0$, and the completion of step 4.1 with $E=\rho=0$ is the zero field; $\mu_0>0$ is fixed and nondegenerate.
The construction is componentwise over three indices and uses no counting family; the derivative identity $D^\alpha A_i=\mu_0N(D^\alpha J_i)$ of step 1.1 requires no choice of an index family.

The Newtonian kernel is singular only at $y=x$, handled by the supplier of step 1.1; no degenerate ball or radius is used, and the Coulomb gauge is a declared construction choice rather than a uniqueness claim, as recorded in step 5.1.

The construction is on all of $\mathbb R^3$ with no boundary data; the time interval $I$ of step 4.1 is an arbitrary open interval, and the completion uses time-independent fields, so no endpoint value is asserted.
Countable Choice is assumed in the Statement and used only through the Newtonian-potential supplier of step 1.1, as recorded in step 5.1; the vector identities of steps 3.1 are choice-free.

boundaries.reason: The theorem constructs a potential satisfying the pair; it asserts no if-and-only-if statement.
No converse and no uniqueness claim is made: step 5.1 states explicitly that neither $A$ nor $B$ is asserted unique.

Assume Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), with the exact meaning of [[def-countable-choice]]. Let $f\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$ and define componentwise
$$A_i(x):=\frac1{4\pi}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{f_i(y)}{|x-y|}\,dy,\qquad A:=(A_1,A_2,A_3),\qquad x\in\mathbb R^3,$$
so that $A=N(f)$ componentwise with the Newtonian-potential transform $N$ of [[lem-em-smooth-newtonian-upgrade]] and [[def-newtonian-potential]]. Then $A\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$, both integrals below are absolutely convergent for every $x$, and for every $x\in\mathbb R^3$
$$\operatorname{div}A(x)=N(\operatorname{div}f)(x)=\frac1{4\pi}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{(\operatorname{div}f)(y)}{|x-y|}\,dy,$$
$$\operatorname{curl}A(x)=\frac1{4\pi}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{f(y)\times(x-y)}{|x-y|^3}\,dy .$$
The curl identity needs no divergence-free hypothesis and holds pointwise at every point of $\mathbb R^3$, including points of the support of $f$; the kernel is differentiated, its smoothness at the pole is not assumed. Countable Choice is used only through the polar-coordinate and surface-measure interfaces of the estimates.

For the Lebesgue/surface/distributional source and admissibility branches (c)-(d), assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). The smooth formulation in (a) and the smooth conserved-current predicate in (b) do not themselves use Choice. Let the laboratory region and its chart, the field and source objects and the units be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], [[def-em-fields]], [[def-em-sources]] and [[def-em-si-conventions]], and fix $\mu_0>0$, $c>0$, $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$.

**(a) [Steady-current regime].** A steady-current (magnetostatic) configuration on $\Omega\times I$ consists of a field pair $E,B:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ and source fields $\rho:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R$, $J:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ that are independent of $t$ and satisfy the smooth branch of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] with the operators of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] and [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]. For such a configuration the formal distributional branch of [[pthm-em-charge-continuity]] gives $\operatorname{div}J=0$ distributionally; this is pointwise when $J$ is $C^1$. In the jointly $C^2$ field/$C^1$ source branch its classical proof applies directly. The locally integrable distributional reading here inherits Countable Choice, whereas the stated classical $C^2/C^1$ compatibility calculation is choice-free, and the four adopted equations are equivalent to the electrostatic pair and the magnetostatic pair
$$\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0,\qquad \operatorname{curl}E=0,\qquad \operatorname{div}B=0,\qquad \operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J .$$

**(b) [Compact smooth current class].** The compact smooth current class of this framework consists of the currents $J\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ with $\operatorname{div}J=0$, extended by zero to $\mathbb R^3$. A magnetostatic field of such a current is a field $B$ of class $C^1$ on $\mathbb R^3$ satisfying $\operatorname{div}B=0$ and $\operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J$ on $\mathbb R^3$ with the extended $J$. This is the hypothesis class of the vector-potential, Biot-Savart and dipole theorems of this page; this definition asserts neither existence nor uniqueness of $B$ in the class.

**(c) [Ideal source objects].** Define three ideal current source objects outside the compact class, together with the data selecting their fields.

**(c1) [Closed thin loop].** For a closed embedded $C^2$ curve $\gamma:\mathbb R/L\mathbb Z\to\mathbb R^3$ with $|\gamma'|\equiv1$ ($L>0$) and $I\in\mathbb R$, the ideal loop current is the distribution
$$\langle J_\gamma,\psi\rangle:=I\int_0^L\gamma'(s)\cdot\psi(\gamma(s))\,ds,\qquad \psi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3),$$
with $\rho_\gamma:=0$.

**(c2) [Infinite straight wire].** For $\gamma(s)=(0,0,s)$, $s\in\mathbb R$, and $I\in\mathbb R$, the ideal wire current is
$$\langle J_{\rm w},\psi\rangle:=I\int_{\mathbb R}\psi_3(0,0,s)\,ds,$$
with $\rho_{\rm w}:=0$.

**(c3) [Infinite cylindrical sheet].** For $a>0$, $S=\{\rho=a\}$, $\rho=\sqrt{x_1^2+x_2^2}$, and $K\in\mathbb R$, the ideal solenoid sheet current is
$$\langle J_S,\psi\rangle:=K\int_S e_\varphi\cdot\psi\,dS$$
([[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]], read on compact cylinder segments), with $\rho_S:=0$. All three pairings are finite because $\psi$ has compact support.

**(c4) [Admissibility].** A field $B$ is admitted for one of these declared models when: $B$ is locally integrable on $\mathbb R^3$ (hence a distribution by [[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]], [[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]]) and $C^1$ off the support of the current; $\operatorname{div}B=0$ and $\operatorname{curl}B=0$ hold pointwise off that support; the distributional identities $\operatorname{div}B=0$ and $\operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J$ hold against every scalar divergence test $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$ and vector curl test $\psi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$ in the sense of [[def-distributional-derivative]]; $B$ has the model's declared symmetry (invariance under translations along and rotations about the axis in (c2) and (c3); no symmetry is required in (c1)); and $B$ obeys the decay requirement: $|B(x)|\to0$ as $|x|\to\infty$ in (c1), and in (c2), (c3) the supremum of $|B|$ over every compact set of cross-sectional parameters tends to $0$ as the transverse radius $\rho\to\infty$. The companion examples exhibit and verify the fields of the two axisymmetric models in this class; the definition itself asserts no existence, uniqueness, finite energy or limiting relation for the declared models, and no compact-class theorem of this page applies to them.

**(d) [Scope].** This is a model restriction: the steady-current regime for compact smooth currents, and three explicitly declared ideal noncompact or singular models. It excludes point charges, weaker-regularity volume sources, moving sheets, normal sheet currents and any claim of empirical exactness; the equations in (c4) define a mathematical admissibility predicate; its physical adoption for these source objects is a separate postulate, and no product of distributions is formed.

For $u=(u_x,u_y,u_z)$ and $v=(v_x,v_y,v_z)$ in $\mathbb R^3$, define $u\times v=(u_yv_z-u_zv_y,\,u_zv_x-u_xv_z,\,u_xv_y-u_yv_x)$.

This is the right-handed **cross product**. The displayed coordinates are those of the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), and inner products and norms are those of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let
$f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable, and let $E\in\mathcal A$. Since
[[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]]
implies that $f\chi_E$ is measurable, define the **integral of $f$ over $E$**
by
$$\int_E f\,d\mu:=\int f\chi_E\,d\mu,$$
where the integral on the right is the nonnegative Lebesgue integral of
[[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]].

If $f\in L^1(\mu)$, then
$$\left|\int f\,d\mu\right|\le\int |f|\,d\mu.$$

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), with the exact meaning of [[def-countable-choice]]. Let $\gamma:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$ be a closed embedded $C^2$ curve parametrized by arc length with period $L>0$: $\gamma(s+L)=\gamma(s)$ and $|\gamma'(s)|=1$ for every $s$, and the induced map $\mathbb R/L\mathbb Z\to\mathbb R^3$ is injective. Let $I\in\mathbb R$ and $\mu_0>0$, and for $\psi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C^3)=:\mathcal D(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C^3)$ ([[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]) define

$$j(\psi)=I\int_0^L\gamma'(s)\cdot\psi(\gamma(s))\,ds,$$

with the complex-bilinear Euclidean pairing (no conjugation) of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]; restricted to real-valued $\psi$ this is the stated real functional. Then $\operatorname{div}j=0$ in the distributional sense ([[def-distributional-derivative]], [[def-distribution]]). For any family $(\eta_\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon>0}$ of nonnegative smooth radial kernels with $\int_{\mathbb R^3}\eta_\varepsilon=1$ and $\operatorname{supp}\eta_\varepsilon\subseteq\overline B_\varepsilon(0)$ — including the rescalings $\eta_\varepsilon(x)=\varepsilon^{-3}\eta(x/\varepsilon)$ of a chosen nonnegative unit-mass radial kernel supported in $\overline B_1(0)$ — the mollified fields $j_\varepsilon$ defined by the distribution pairing $j_\varepsilon(x):=j(\eta_\varepsilon(x-\cdot))=I\int_0^L\gamma'(s)\eta_\varepsilon(x-\gamma(s))\,ds$ are smooth, compactly supported and divergence-free, and their Biot-Savart fields converge, with every derivative uniformly on every nonempty compact $K\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ disjoint from $\gamma$, to

$$B(x)=\frac{\mu_0I}{4\pi}\int_0^L\frac{\gamma'(s)\times(x-\gamma(s))}{|x-\gamma(s)|^3}\,ds$$

([[def-cross-product-in-r3]]). In addition, assigning arbitrary finite values on the curve gives a representative $B\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$, smooth off $\gamma$, with $\operatorname{div}T_B=0$ and $\operatorname{curl}T_B=\mu_0j$ globally; the first identity is tested on scalar $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$ and the second on vector $\psi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C^3)$. If $\gamma([0,L])\subseteq B_a(0)$ for some $a>0$, then $|B(x)|\le\mu_0|I|L/\bigl(4\pi(|x|-a)^2\bigr)$ for $|x|>a$, so $B$ decays at infinity. For the circle $\gamma(s)=a(\cos(s/a),\sin(s/a),0)$ and a point $z e_3$ on its axis the value is $B_z=\mu_0Ia^2/\bigl(2(a^2+z^2)^{3/2}\bigr)$. Nothing is asserted about the divergent line self-energy or about fields on the curve itself.

Assume Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), with the exact meaning of [[def-countable-choice]]. In the named inertial laboratory model of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], with the positive constants and SI conventions of [[def-em-si-conventions]], adopt the following additional classical physical idealization: a loop, infinite straight line or infinite cylindrical sheet source defined by [[def-em-steady-current-regime]](c1)-(c3), with zero charge density, is modeled by a time-independent $B$ satisfying exactly the admissibility predicate (c4), together with $E=0$ and $\rho=0$. Thus $\operatorname{div}B=0$ and $\operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J$ hold distributionally on $\mathbb R^3$, with the stated off-source regularity, symmetry and decay; the electrostatic and temporal Maxwell identities are zero. This physical adoption extends to these explicitly declared source types only. It is separate from the earlier $L^1$-source and point/compact-sheet postulates, which do not include these line and noncompact sheet sources. No existence, uniqueness, finite self-energy, force product, self-force, apparatus accuracy, matter dynamics or empirical certainty is asserted.

derivations.claim: By [F1], $B=\operatorname{curl}A$ with $A_i=\mu_0N(J_i)$. Applying [F2] to $f:=J$ and multiplying by $\mu_0$ gives, at every $x\in\mathbb R^3$, $B(x)=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{J(y)\times(x-y)}{|x-y|^3}\,dy$, with the integral absolutely convergent by the estimate $|J(y)\times(x-y)|\le\|J\|_\infty|x-y|$ and $\int_{B_R(x)}|x-y|^{-2}d\lambda_3<+\infty$ for a ball containing $\operatorname{supp}J$; this proves the first assertion at every point, including points of the support of $J$.

By [F3], the tangent line current $j$ of the declared loop is divergence-free, its mollified currents $j_\varepsilon$ are smooth, compactly supported and divergence-free, so each $j_\varepsilon$ is a compact smooth conserved current of the class [F4](b); step 1.1 applied with $J:=j_\varepsilon$ identifies the field of $j_\varepsilon$ with its displayed Biot-Savart integral. The supplier's every-derivative uniform convergence on every compact $K$ disjoint from $\gamma$ therefore identifies the limit field with $B_\gamma(x)=\frac{\mu_0I}{4\pi}\int_0^L\frac{\gamma'(s)\times(x-\gamma(s))}{|x-\gamma(s)|^3}\,ds$ on the complement of $\gamma$.

The same supplier [F3] supplies, independently of the away-from-curve convergence, the globally locally integrable representative of $B_\gamma$ on $\mathbb R^3$, its smoothness off $\gamma$, the global distributional identities $\operatorname{div}T_{B_\gamma}=0$ and $\operatorname{curl}T_{B_\gamma}=\mu_0j$, and the decay bound. Together with the symmetry requirement (vacuous for the loop clause) these are exactly the clauses of the admissibility predicate [F4](c4), so $B_\gamma$ is an admitted field of the declared ideal thin loop; the physical reading of that declaration is the separate adopted assumption [F5], which asserts no existence, uniqueness, self-energy or force content.

Clauses (a) and (b) of the Statement are steps 1.1 and 2.1-3.1; the scope clause records that no formula is asserted for noncompact currents (the infinite-wire model is verified separately on the companion examples page), and that no near-wire, self-energy, radiation or force claim is made. Countable Choice is inherited only through the cited measure, regular-distribution and Newtonian supplier interfaces [F7]; no stronger choice principle occurs.

The zero-current and zero-amplitude cases are the cases $J=0$ and $I=0$ of steps 1.1 and 2.1; the mollified fields of the zero current are zero, and the limit field vanishes identically.

One current and one loop are fixed; no counting family appears, and the mollifier family is indexed by a single positive parameter $\varepsilon$; the case is read off the Statement and step 1.1 of the item.

The loop is closed and has no endpoints; the convergence assertion is on compacts $K$ disjoint from $\gamma$, so the curve itself and its neighbourhood are excluded rather than treated as an endpoint case; the case is read off the Statement and step 1.1 of the item.
Countable Choice is assumed and inherited from the differentiated-kernel lemma of step 1.1 and the thin-current supplier of steps 2.1 and 3.1; no additional selection occurs.

No converse is claimed: the theorem does not assert that every field with $\operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J$ is given by the displayed integral.

Let the compact smooth current class and the declared ideal models be those of [[def-em-steady-current-regime]], with the units of [[def-em-si-conventions]].

**(a) [Compact smooth currents].** Let $J\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ with $\operatorname{div}J=0$, extended by zero to $\mathbb R^3$. The **magnetic dipole moment** of $J$ is the vector
$$m:=\frac12\int_{\mathbb R^3}y\times J(y)\,dy\in\mathbb R^3,$$
of unit A m$^2$. The integral is computed componentwise over any nondegenerate closed bounding rectangle $Q$ containing $\operatorname{supp}J$, using the continuous functions $y\mapsto(y\times J(y))_i$ on $Q$ and their zero extension outside $Q$. Its value is independent of the chosen larger bounding rectangle by finite rectangular subdivision and vanishing of the integrand off its support; the support itself need not be Jordan measurable. Thus this is a Riemann integral of continuous compactly supported functions ([[def-riemann-integral-over-a-jordan-set]], [[thm-continuous-functions-on-compact-jordan-sets-are-integrable]], [[def-cross-product-in-r3]]); it is absolutely finite because $J$ is bounded with compact support.

**(b) [Declared ideal thin loop].** For a closed embedded $C^2$ curve $\gamma:\mathbb R/L\mathbb Z\to\mathbb R^3$ with $|\gamma'|\equiv1$ and $I\in\mathbb R$, the **magnetic moment** of the ideal loop current of [[def-em-steady-current-regime]](c1) is
$$m:=\frac I2\int_0^L\gamma(s)\times\gamma'(s)\,ds,$$
again a componentwise Riemann integral over the compact interval $[0,L]$ of continuous functions; for the circle $\gamma(s)=a(\cos(s/a),\sin(s/a),0)$ traversed in the positive orientation this is $m=I\pi a^2e_3$.

**(c) [Status and scope].** In both clauses $m$ is a source moment of the declared current model: it is not a rest mass, not an intrinsic spin and not an observed quantity. The definition asserts no far-field property of $m$ (that is the content of [[pthm-em-magnetic-dipole-field]] under its hypotheses), no agreement between the two clauses in a common limit, and no moment for currents outside the two classes; no higher multipole is defined here. The finite Riemann moment definitions and circular-loop evaluation themselves are choice-free; no distribution-embedding or surface-measure theorem is used to compute these moments.

For $u=(u_x,u_y,u_z)$ and $v=(v_x,v_y,v_z)$ in $\mathbb R^3$, define $u\times v=(u_yv_z-u_zv_y,\,u_zv_x-u_xv_z,\,u_xv_y-u_yv_x)$.

This is the right-handed **cross product**. The displayed coordinates are those of the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), and inner products and norms are those of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].

Assume Countable Choice. Let $Q=\prod_{i=1}^n[a_i,b_i]$ with $n\ge1$ and $a_i<b_i$. If a bounded Borel real function $f$ on $Q$ is Riemann integrable, then it is Lebesgue integrable and the two integrals agree. The corresponding assertion for complex functions holds componentwise. In particular it applies to smooth compact test integrands and their bounded Borel zero extensions from compact Jordan regions.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), with the exact meaning of [[def-countable-choice]]. Let $\mu_0>0$ be any scalar parameter and let $J\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$ with $\operatorname{div}J=0$ and $\operatorname{supp}J\subset B_a(0)$, $a>0$, and put $m=\tfrac12\int_{\mathbb R^3}y\times J(y)\,dy$ ([[def-cross-product-in-r3]]). Then for $r=|x|\ge2a$ the vector potential and magnetic field $$A(x)=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{J(y)}{|x-y|}\,dy,\qquad B=\operatorname{curl}A,$$ satisfy, uniformly in $n=x/r$, $$A=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{m\times x}{r^3}+O\!\Bigl(\frac{\mu_0a^2\|J\|_1}{r^3}\Bigr),\qquad B=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{3n(m\cdot n)-m}{r^3}+O\!\Bigl(\frac{\mu_0a^2\|J\|_1}{r^4}\Bigr).$$ The constants in the $O$ terms are absolute (the second follows by differentiating the first, not by differentiating an unspecified remainder), and $\|J\|_1=\int|J|$.

derivations.claim: The hypotheses of [F3] are exactly the hypotheses stated here for $J$ (smooth, compactly supported, divergence-free, contained in $B_a(0)$), and the objects of [F3] are the objects of this theorem: $A=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\int J(y)|x-y|^{-1}dy$ componentwise and $B=\operatorname{curl}A$ by [F1]. The moment of [F2] agrees with the Lebesgue moment of [F3]: each component $y\mapsto(y\times J(y))_i$ is smooth and compactly supported, hence bounded Borel and Riemann integrable on any nondegenerate closed rectangle $Q$ containing $\operatorname{supp}J$; by [F4] its Riemann integral over $Q$ equals its Lebesgue integral over $Q$, and since the integrand vanishes off $\operatorname{supp}J\subset Q$ this equals the Lebesgue integral over $\mathbb R^3$. Hence $\frac12\int_{\mathbb R^3}y\times J(y)\,dy$ is the same vector in both items.

Substituting the identifications of step 1.1 into the conclusion of [F3] gives, for $r=|x|\ge2a$ and uniformly in the unit vector $n=x/r$, the displayed estimates $A(x)=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{m\times x}{r^3}+O(\mu_0a^2\|J\|_1r^{-3})$ and $B(x)=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{3n(m\cdot n)-m}{r^3}+O(\mu_0a^2\|J\|_1r^{-4})$ for the framework's $A$ and $B$, with the lemma's uniformity and absolute constants and with $\|J\|_1=\int_{\mathbb R^3}|J|\,d\lambda_3$ as in the Statement.

The estimates of step 2.1 are the content of the Statement; no assertion is made for $r<2a$ or at the support, no higher multipole is defined, and the leading dipole term is not claimed to be exact. Countable Choice is used only through the Riemann-Lebesgue comparison [F4] and the measure and Newtonian interfaces [F5] of the cited suppliers; no stronger choice principle occurs.

boundaries.evidence: For $J=0$ the moment vanishes and both displays of step 2.1 reduce to $0=0$ plus a vanishing remainder; no nonempty support is required.
The zero case includes $J=0$ and $m=0$ with $a>0$ fixed; step 1.1 shows the moment of the definition equals the Lebesgue moment, and the leading terms in step 2.1 carry the factor $m$.

One current and one moment are fixed; no counting family appears, and the estimates use only the single radius parameter $a$ and the point $x$; the case is read off the Statement and step 1.1 of the item.

The hypotheses require $\operatorname{supp}J\subset B_a(0)$ with $a>0$ and $r=|x|\ge2a$, so no degenerate ball appears; the degenerate value $m=0$ is permitted and covered by the estimate; the case is read off the Statement and step 1.1 of the item.
The threshold $r=2a$ is included by the statement $r\ge2a$ and both displays hold there; no assertion is made for $r<2a$ or at points of the support, as recorded in step 3.1.
Countable Choice is assumed and used only through the Riemann-Lebesgue comparison of step 1.1 and the measure and Newtonian interfaces of the cited suppliers, as recorded in step 3.1.

No converse is claimed: the far-field form is not asserted to determine the source or its moment.

Let $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be bounded in the metric sense of
[[def-metric-bounded-diameter]] and Jordan measurable, and let
$f:E\to\mathbb R$ be bounded. Choose a nondegenerate rectangle
$Q\supseteq E$, whose existence follows from
[[def-jordan-inner-and-outer-content]], and define the zero extension
$$\widetilde f_Q(x):=\begin{cases}f(x),&x\in E,\\0,&x\in Q\setminus E.\end{cases}$$
The function $f$ is **Riemann integrable over $E$** when $\widetilde f_Q$ is integrable over $Q$, and then
$$\int_Ef:=\int_Q\widetilde f_Q.$$
Independence of the bounding rectangle, for both integrability and value, is proved in [[lem-jordan-set-integral-well-defined]] and recorded as the definition's forward justification. For $f=1$, the zero extension is $1_E$, so [[thm-jordan-content-and-indicator-integrability]] gives $\int_E1=\operatorname{cont}(E)$.
Every continuous real function on a compact Jordan measurable set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is Riemann integrable over $E$.

Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $m,q\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$. A map $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$ is of class $C^k$ when each component is of class $C^k$. Each scalar component uses the word-derivative convention of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], whose source dimension is positive. The map is **smooth**, or $C^\infty$, when it is $C^k$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $U,V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open. A bijection $f:U\to V$ is a **$C^k$ diffeomorphism** when both $f$ and $f^{-1}$ are $C^k$. For $k\ge1$, a **local $C^k$ diffeomorphism at $a\in U$** is a restriction $f|_P:P\to Q$ between open neighbourhoods of $a$ and $f(a)$ that is a $C^k$ diffeomorphism. At $k=1$ this agrees with [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]]: continuous first partial derivatives give the required total derivative by [[thm-continuous-partial-derivatives-imply-total-differentiability]], while continuity of the total derivative gives continuity of its matrix entries and hence of the first partial derivatives.

For $u=(u_x,u_y,u_z)$ and $v=(v_x,v_y,v_z)$ in $\mathbb R^3$, define $u\times v=(u_yv_z-u_zv_y,\,u_zv_x-u_xv_z,\,u_xv_y-u_yv_x)$.

This is the right-handed **cross product**. The displayed coordinates are those of the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), and inner products and norms are those of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Let $Q=\prod_{j<m}[a_j,b_j]$ be nondegenerate. For integrable
$f,g:Q\to\mathbb R$ and scalars $\alpha,\beta$, the function
$\alpha f+\beta g$ is integrable and its integral is
$\alpha\int_Qf+\beta\int_Qg$. If $f\le g$, then
$\int_Qf\le\int_Qg$. Also $|f|$ is integrable and
$|\int_Qf|\le\int_Q|f|$. If $a_r<c<b_r$, cutting $Q$ at the coordinate
hyperplane $x_r=c$ gives two nondegenerate subrectangles; integrability on
$Q$ is equivalent to integrability on both restrictions, and their integral
values add to the integral over $Q$.

Let $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be bounded in the metric sense of
[[def-metric-bounded-diameter]] and Jordan measurable, and let
$f:E\to\mathbb R$ be bounded. Choose a nondegenerate rectangle
$Q\supseteq E$, whose existence follows from
[[def-jordan-inner-and-outer-content]], and define the zero extension
$$\widetilde f_Q(x):=\begin{cases}f(x),&x\in E,\\0,&x\in Q\setminus E.\end{cases}$$
The function $f$ is **Riemann integrable over $E$** when $\widetilde f_Q$ is integrable over $Q$, and then
$$\int_Ef:=\int_Q\widetilde f_Q.$$
Independence of the bounding rectangle, for both integrability and value, is proved in [[lem-jordan-set-integral-well-defined]] and recorded as the definition's forward justification. For $f=1$, the zero extension is $1_E$, so [[thm-jordan-content-and-indicator-integrability]] gives $\int_E1=\operatorname{cont}(E)$.

Let the compact smooth current class and the declared ideal models be those of [[def-em-steady-current-regime]], with the units of [[def-em-si-conventions]].

**(a) [Compact smooth currents].** Let $J\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ with $\operatorname{div}J=0$, extended by zero to $\mathbb R^3$. The **magnetic dipole moment** of $J$ is the vector
$$m:=\frac12\int_{\mathbb R^3}y\times J(y)\,dy\in\mathbb R^3,$$
of unit A m$^2$. The integral is computed componentwise over any nondegenerate closed bounding rectangle $Q$ containing $\operatorname{supp}J$, using the continuous functions $y\mapsto(y\times J(y))_i$ on $Q$ and their zero extension outside $Q$. Its value is independent of the chosen larger bounding rectangle by finite rectangular subdivision and vanishing of the integrand off its support; the support itself need not be Jordan measurable. Thus this is a Riemann integral of continuous compactly supported functions ([[def-riemann-integral-over-a-jordan-set]], [[thm-continuous-functions-on-compact-jordan-sets-are-integrable]], [[def-cross-product-in-r3]]); it is absolutely finite because $J$ is bounded with compact support.

**(b) [Declared ideal thin loop].** For a closed embedded $C^2$ curve $\gamma:\mathbb R/L\mathbb Z\to\mathbb R^3$ with $|\gamma'|\equiv1$ and $I\in\mathbb R$, the **magnetic moment** of the ideal loop current of [[def-em-steady-current-regime]](c1) is
$$m:=\frac I2\int_0^L\gamma(s)\times\gamma'(s)\,ds,$$
again a componentwise Riemann integral over the compact interval $[0,L]$ of continuous functions; for the circle $\gamma(s)=a(\cos(s/a),\sin(s/a),0)$ traversed in the positive orientation this is $m=I\pi a^2e_3$.

**(c) [Status and scope].** In both clauses $m$ is a source moment of the declared current model: it is not a rest mass, not an intrinsic spin and not an observed quantity. The definition asserts no far-field property of $m$ (that is the content of [[pthm-em-magnetic-dipole-field]] under its hypotheses), no agreement between the two clauses in a common limit, and no moment for currents outside the two classes; no higher multipole is defined here. The finite Riemann moment definitions and circular-loop evaluation themselves are choice-free; no distribution-embedding or surface-measure theorem is used to compute these moments.

For the Lebesgue/surface/distributional source and admissibility branches (c)-(d), assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). The smooth formulation in (a) and the smooth conserved-current predicate in (b) do not themselves use Choice. Let the laboratory region and its chart, the field and source objects and the units be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], [[def-em-fields]], [[def-em-sources]] and [[def-em-si-conventions]], and fix $\mu_0>0$, $c>0$, $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$.

**(a) [Steady-current regime].** A steady-current (magnetostatic) configuration on $\Omega\times I$ consists of a field pair $E,B:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ and source fields $\rho:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R$, $J:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ that are independent of $t$ and satisfy the smooth branch of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] with the operators of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] and [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]. For such a configuration the formal distributional branch of [[pthm-em-charge-continuity]] gives $\operatorname{div}J=0$ distributionally; this is pointwise when $J$ is $C^1$. In the jointly $C^2$ field/$C^1$ source branch its classical proof applies directly. The locally integrable distributional reading here inherits Countable Choice, whereas the stated classical $C^2/C^1$ compatibility calculation is choice-free, and the four adopted equations are equivalent to the electrostatic pair and the magnetostatic pair
$$\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0,\qquad \operatorname{curl}E=0,\qquad \operatorname{div}B=0,\qquad \operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J .$$

**(b) [Compact smooth current class].** The compact smooth current class of this framework consists of the currents $J\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ with $\operatorname{div}J=0$, extended by zero to $\mathbb R^3$. A magnetostatic field of such a current is a field $B$ of class $C^1$ on $\mathbb R^3$ satisfying $\operatorname{div}B=0$ and $\operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J$ on $\mathbb R^3$ with the extended $J$. This is the hypothesis class of the vector-potential, Biot-Savart and dipole theorems of this page; this definition asserts neither existence nor uniqueness of $B$ in the class.

**(c) [Ideal source objects].** Define three ideal current source objects outside the compact class, together with the data selecting their fields.

**(c1) [Closed thin loop].** For a closed embedded $C^2$ curve $\gamma:\mathbb R/L\mathbb Z\to\mathbb R^3$ with $|\gamma'|\equiv1$ ($L>0$) and $I\in\mathbb R$, the ideal loop current is the distribution
$$\langle J_\gamma,\psi\rangle:=I\int_0^L\gamma'(s)\cdot\psi(\gamma(s))\,ds,\qquad \psi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3),$$
with $\rho_\gamma:=0$.

**(c2) [Infinite straight wire].** For $\gamma(s)=(0,0,s)$, $s\in\mathbb R$, and $I\in\mathbb R$, the ideal wire current is
$$\langle J_{\rm w},\psi\rangle:=I\int_{\mathbb R}\psi_3(0,0,s)\,ds,$$
with $\rho_{\rm w}:=0$.

**(c3) [Infinite cylindrical sheet].** For $a>0$, $S=\{\rho=a\}$, $\rho=\sqrt{x_1^2+x_2^2}$, and $K\in\mathbb R$, the ideal solenoid sheet current is
$$\langle J_S,\psi\rangle:=K\int_S e_\varphi\cdot\psi\,dS$$
([[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]], read on compact cylinder segments), with $\rho_S:=0$. All three pairings are finite because $\psi$ has compact support.

**(c4) [Admissibility].** A field $B$ is admitted for one of these declared models when: $B$ is locally integrable on $\mathbb R^3$ (hence a distribution by [[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]], [[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]]) and $C^1$ off the support of the current; $\operatorname{div}B=0$ and $\operatorname{curl}B=0$ hold pointwise off that support; the distributional identities $\operatorname{div}B=0$ and $\operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J$ hold against every scalar divergence test $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$ and vector curl test $\psi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$ in the sense of [[def-distributional-derivative]]; $B$ has the model's declared symmetry (invariance under translations along and rotations about the axis in (c2) and (c3); no symmetry is required in (c1)); and $B$ obeys the decay requirement: $|B(x)|\to0$ as $|x|\to\infty$ in (c1), and in (c2), (c3) the supremum of $|B|$ over every compact set of cross-sectional parameters tends to $0$ as the transverse radius $\rho\to\infty$. The companion examples exhibit and verify the fields of the two axisymmetric models in this class; the definition itself asserts no existence, uniqueness, finite energy or limiting relation for the declared models, and no compact-class theorem of this page applies to them.

**(d) [Scope].** This is a model restriction: the steady-current regime for compact smooth currents, and three explicitly declared ideal noncompact or singular models. It excludes point charges, weaker-regularity volume sources, moving sheets, normal sheet currents and any claim of empirical exactness; the equations in (c4) define a mathematical admissibility predicate; its physical adoption for these source objects is a separate postulate, and no product of distributions is formed.
